title: From genes to neurons to brain
abstract: Molecular biological approaches have played a key role in our growing understanding of nervous system function in health and disease. However, coupling individual molecular events with the function of distributed neural systems involved in complex behaviors and neuropsychiatric diseases requires the integration of reductionist molecular work with systems neuroscience. Genetic and genomic methods can help provide a systems context for individual molecular changes and also serve as a bridge between human biology and animal or cell models. For example, once genes are identified as causal or susceptibility factors in human disease, the appropriate use of animal or in vitro models will play a key role in clarifying the structural and functional changes occurring at the cellular and neural systems levels. In contrast, when the underlying circuits are well connected to a particular conserved cognitive function or behavior, work in the animal models to define the molecular etiologies can be appropriately translated to humans. With regard to both of these approaches, the manuscripts in this supplement that highlight several presentations from the advanced course ‘Genes and Neurons’ (held in July 2004 at the University of Minho, Braga, Portugal) share a common theme of bridging the gulf between genes and behavior. These papers reflect an area of research that is emerging as one of broad interest to the neuroscience community, as it represents recent advances that bridge the gap between genes, brain and behavior, in many cases using animal models to help shed light on complex human behaviors or cognition and disorders that affect these processes. This ‘Genes and Neurons’ supplement provides a broad overview of this area, covering both fundamental and hot topics, ranging from the basics of mouse behavior and cognition (Sousa, Almeida and Wotjak), genetic approaches to common psychiatric diseases (van Belzen and Heutink), to the MAP kinase (MapK) pathway in memory (Davis and Laroche), the genetics and neurobiology of mental retardation (MR) (Dierssen and Ramakers), the molecular basis of circadian behavior (Oster), a molecular systems level approach to anxiety (Stoppel, Albrecht, Pape and Stork), chromatin remodeling and developmental disorders (Santos and Maciel) and Alzheimer′ Dementia (Grazina and Oliveira). As such, this issue provides an extremely worthwhile and up to date review of these core topics in the molecular genetic basis of cognition and behavior for students and experts alike. In the comprehensively referenced ‘A hitchhiker's guide to behavioral analysis in laboratory rodents', Sousa and colleagues take on the difficult job of providing a template for approaching analysis of relevant behaviors in rats and mice. Several key points are worth noting. Sousa et al. emphasize the importance of using qualitative and quantitative strain differences in genetic mapping, and the challenges of moving from quantitative trait loci (QTLs) to genes, highlighting the development of more sophisticated and innovative analytic methods to facilitate these efforts. They focus on many critical practical issues that can impede proper assessment of behavior in mice, such as handling, training, stable routines and the failure to appreciate interstrain differences. Sousa et al. also appropriately caution us to be wary of over-interpreting molecular lesion studies, such as single-gene knockouts. Similar to anatomical lesion studies of the brain in developing animals, the functions being measured not only reflect the absence of a particular gene but also the potential consequences of environmental factors and molecular or behavioral systems' adaptations to the insult, including the use of alternative strategies not relevant to normal development or function. Lastly, they provide a practical guide for the general assessment of behavior, physical features and cognition in mice. It is clear from this extensive guide that although some of the areas such as motor behavior and memory are well established, several areas of particular relevance to human disease, for example, social behavior (of particular relevance to autism), are far less developed. Furthermore, how aberrancies in native social behaviors in mice correspond to human neurobehavioral disorders is a largely unexplored area. In a parallel introductory chapter, van Belzen and Heutink provide an exceptionally clear and thorough introduction on the use of modern genetic mapping tools to identify genes causing human psychiatric disorders. They move from explaining notions of heritability, the challenge of mapping complex disease genes and endophenotypes to providing concrete examples of approaches that have worked in defining genetic susceptibility factors in complex diseases, such as schizophrenia. Van Belzen and Heutink discuss linkage, association, candidate genes and issues of phenotype definition in a manner that is accessible to even the genetically unsophisticated audience, and as such this paper is highly recommended reading for those wanting a comprehensive introduction to this topic. They cite a number of advances in the genetics of psychiatric disorders, including work on Disc-1, Disbindin and other genes underlying genetic risk for schizophrenia that support their optimistic assessment of the outlook for the field of human psychiatric genetics. Here, the field has already made the jump successfully from humans to animal models in some cases. One of the neural circuits underlying complex behavior that has been extensively studied over the last two decades involves brain regions mediating fear and anxiety, which consist of highly conserved pathways that are very amenable to modeling in rodents. As Stoppel et al. note in their article ‘Genes and Neurons: Molecular Insight into Anxiety’, anxiety disorders and related conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), while having a heritable component in humans, are complex genetic conditions likely involving multiple genes interacting with the environment. Stoppel and colleagues appropriately champion the use of animal models, which allow molecular dissection of this circuitry, one gene at a time. They point out that studying these mouse models has allowed molecular dissection of molecules that modulate anxiety in the mouse, which has in turn clearly informed our understanding of human disease. In the case of fear conditioning, the knowledge of the behavior, circuitry and some initial molecular clues allowed for productive exploitation of this system in rodents to understand human anxiety in disease. QTL mapping in mouse has identified several loci that modulate distinct aspects of this process, and these loci can be compared with those identified in human conditions to help identify genes. Similarly, genes that modulate mouse behavior become candidates in studies of humans. This translational work is in its beginning, but the authors make it clear that the genes and systems already identified will be fruitful for understanding human genetic variation, perhaps related to PTSD and other debilitating neuropsychiatric disorders. Furthermore, because anxiety is such a prominent symptom in many human brain disorders, including dementia and developmental conditions such as Fragile X syndrome, better molecular targeting of this symptom domain is of great public health importance. The concept of MR as a phenotype driving genetic studies is controversial from the standpoint of modern cognitive neuroscience, which often emphasizes the study of discrete cognitive processes and the specific neural circuits that are their basis. However, from the standpoint of both public health impact and human genetics, MR syndromes are illustrative of success in multiple domains of the mouse model from gene identification and diagnostic testing to modeling. Dierssen and Ramakers highlight the phenomenon of dendritic pathology as a unifying feature across syndromes and across species. Such a neuropathological endophenotype is optimal for cross-species translation. These authors discuss the common pathology observed in MR as possibly affecting ‘communication systems’ in a global fashion across the brain. In this particular case, it is not clear precisely which anatomical or physiological substrates the authors are referring to by the terminology ‘communication systems.’ Perhaps, they mean to liken MR to a global disconnection syndrome involving higher order association areas, a concept that serves as one of the foundations of modern behavioral neurology (Catani & ffytche 2005; Geschwind 1965a, b). In this context, defects in axon pathfinding, neuronal migration or placement, synaptic plasticity and signaling properties of neurons all could lead to similar phenotypes, in which most primary sensory systems function, but carefully timed interregional communication of second-order and third-order association areas necessitated by most higher cognitive processes would be impeded. The authors discuss data from animal models of Down syndrome and Fragile X syndrome and in afflicted humans using functional imaging modalities that provide support for this disconnection hypothesis. Should such common processes be involved in rare and diverse forms of MR, it would provide potential for common treatment avenues in the future. In contrast to MR, memory function has been one of the topics explored most by modern cognitive neuroscience. Here, a huge literature on memory function in humans and animal models can be brought to bear on molecular genetic approaches. Homologous systems, from molecules, to regions, to specific forms of memory, have been identified across divergent species, including humans. Davis and Laroche review one of the hottest areas in the molecular basis of memory, the role of MapK signaling pathways in coupling synaptic signals to transcriptional changes that modify neuronal excitability at specific synapses. This is a confusing area to those outside the field, filled with a veritable alphabet soup; hence, although most of us wish to know more about MapK's, ras, rafs and Erks phosphorylate CREBs and other four letter words, this material is often hard to access at some basic, yet current level. Here, the authors not only explain what is known about this cascade in clear detail but also relate it to a wide variety of learning paradigms in model systems, from fear conditioning to object memory. Although the distinction between short-term and long-term memory has been clear at the psychological and anatomical level in primates and mice, the molecular basis of this distinction should be of particular interest for those outside of this rapidly moving field. One of the most interesting and highly conserved systems regulating complex human behavior is the circadian system, in which variation affects most of the other systems covered in this supplement, including memory, anxiety and social behavior. Henrik Oster reviews work in animal systems, including Drosophila, that have informed the study of human circadian behaviors at a molecular level. Oster contrasts the concepts of central vs. peripheral pacemakers, describing how both can be orchestrated in a hierarchical manner. Here, microarray studies have proven valuable, showing that nearly 10% of genes show circadian variability in expression. It is also important to note in the context of translation between animal models and humans that there is emerging data showing that this work has clearly informed human genetics and the molecular basis of sleep and circadian rythms in humans (Lowrey & Takahashi 2004; Xu et al. 2005). Two final papers address mechanisms of disease at the ends of the developmental spectrum, during early childhood and aging. Santos and Maciel review the role of the epigenetic regulation of gene expression in brain function and development. At a molecular level, epigenetic changes involve reversible but often heritable modifications that alter DNA function without changing actual DNA sequence. The role of epigenetics in neurodevelopmental disorders is emphasized by the role of imprinting in Prader–Willi/Angelman syndrome and dysregulation of a canonical form of epigenetic modulation, DNA methylation, in Rett Syndrome. In Rett syndrome, loss-of-function mutations in the global transcriptional regulator, MECP2, cause a striking, regressive and degenerative MR syndrome. Santos and Maciel critically analyze some of the unexpected results of classic microarray experiments performed on MECP2-null animals and provide a clear synthesis of the data on MECP2 targets that is moving to unravel the mystery of Rett pathophysiology. Furthermore, they review several studies that support their view that chromatin structure alterations are likely to play a role in a variety of cognitive and behavioral phenotypes in humans and provide a mechanism whereby environmental factors can have lasting effects on an individual genome and the genetic control of behavior. In the final paper of this supplement, Grazina et al. discuss their hypothesis-driven approach to unravel the genetics of a disease that has been challenging to model in rodents, Alzheimers Disease (AD). They provide an extensive summary of current literature on AD pathophysiology to highlight 12 potential biological pathways. In their synthesis, they elegantly couple an emerging literature on oxidative stress and the function of known Mendelian mutations to findings of energetic deficits in post-mortem AD brains, lending support to the hypothesis that mtDNA mutations may contribute to AD susceptibility. They describe a number of findings in case–control studies identifying potential pathophysiologically relevant changes in mtDNA, including one in the related disorder frontotemporal dementia. The data presented strongly support the biological plausibility of the mitochondrial hypothesis, and the authors provide one of the most scholarly analyses of all of the methodological and technical factors that may confound the results that I have seen. However, as they suggest, the absence of clear maternal inheritance, the non-replication of many findings, in what are mostly small case–control association studies, weakens the genetic support for this otherwise worthy hypothesis. In their critical assessment, the authors provide an ample roadmap for future research in this challenging but important area. The major unstated question looming over animal models of complex cognitive and behavioral human phenotypes is how much can we translate between these species that diverge at every level, from the complexity of cortical regions to single nucleotide polymorphisms. It is clear that even mouse and rat are quite distinct in many aspects of their behavior and brain organization. Yet, little has been done to directly address the relevance of mouse work to human cognition and behavior, presumably because of the complexity of such analyses. This is not to diminish the importance of models but to emphasize the necessity of analyzing data in the appropriate comparative and evolutionary context, so as to enable real progress in our understanding of brain dysfunction in neuropsychiatric disease. Such approaches necessitate development of new tools, and the application of systems biology approaches to permit a true synthetic view of human disease. The review articles included in this supplement were written by invited speakers from the course ”Genes and Neurons”, sponsored by the European Science Foundation, Functional Genomics Programme.

title: Conspiracy of yeast killers: The fifth international meeting on yeast apoptosis in Prague, Czech Republic, 3â7 September, 2006
abstract: It was a unique atmosphere when 60 birds of paradise from all over the world gathered in Kutna Hora, an old silver-digger town near Prague. No justifications, no explanations, no excuses regarding the decision to work on such an exotic topic were offered. Instead, the community, which is almost a family since a core group of people and a growing number of others meet regularly to offer advice and help with plasmids and strains, suddenly realized that a turning point in the field had been reached. Prior to this meeting, most publications had demonstrated that yeast apoptosis (Madeo, 1997) is comparable to mammalian apoptosis. Here, for the first time, the majority of groups presented results that provided new insights into apoptosis research as a whole and that could give new directions to research in other model organisms or cell-culture systems. Chronological ageing of yeast, defined as the lifespan of a postdiauxic but still metabolic active culture, has been used as a valuable model with which to study oxidative damage and molecularly conserved ageing pathways of postmitotic tissues in higher organisms. Replicative ageing, defined by the number of daughters born from a single mother, represents a model for asymmetrically dividing stem cells. Both replicative and chronological ageing of yeast cells have been demonstrated to culminate in cell death with an apoptotic phenotype (Laun, 2001; Fabrizio, 2004; Herker, 2004). It was Ian Dawes (Sydney, Australia) who opened the meeting with an introduction about how reactive oxygen species (ROS) contribute to ageing by damaging nucleic acids, proteins and lipids. In addition, he gave details of a study aiming to evaluate the influence of diverse antioxidants on replicative lifespan and discussed the correlation between oxidative stress and replicative ageing (Laun, 2001). On a more methodological level, David Goldfarb (Rochester, USA) presented the development and initial applications of a new assay for determining replicative lifespan (‘death of daughters’ assay). Here, a genetically engineered yeast strain is used in which the daughters of mother cells die under nonpermissive conditions limiting replicative lifespan to the initial population of mother cells (Jarolim, 2004). He reported on the use of the assay to identify new genes that are required for full lifespan. Gennaro D'Urso (Miami, USA) showed how the method of apoptosis induction by chronological ageing is transferable to fission yeast. Data from this method suggest that DNA replication stress under starvation conditions may be responsible for activation of the cell-death pathway. In a different ageing approach, Kai-Uwe Fröhlich and Christoph Ruckenstuhl (Graz, Austria) presented a new monocolony assay to monitor developmental cell death within whole colonies. Interestingly, mitochondria, the central death-regulating organelles, appear to play a crucial role for cell survival in yeast colonies. Stefan Woelfl and Ana Kitanovic (Heidelberg, Germany) focused on cellular adaptive responses to low doses of toxic substances. In their study, low concentrations of MMS, a DNA-alkylating and thus DNA-damaging agent, triggered an adaptive response induced by the onset of the general stress response mechanism, an increased ROS production, and an intensified metabolic rate. However, this defence response, although it leads to an effective DNA damage repair, also shortens the life-span of the cells. Kitanovic & Wolfl (2006) further demonstrated that regulation of the key enzyme of gluconeogenesis, FBP1, is essential for such a proper response to DNA damage and ageing. Furthermore, rapid ageing upon Fbp1p-overexpression and a requirement for Yca1p or Aif1p, two key players of yeast apoptosis (Madeo, 2002; Wissing, 2004), in this process were shown. Paola Fabrizio (Los Angeles, USA) described a cell death and ageing regulatory network connecting mutations in yeast orthologues of mammalian Ras, Akt and Tor with resistance to stress-induced and age-dependent cell death. These results are beginning to reveal the complexity of a network of proteins involved in the regulation of both ageing and age-dependent cell death conserved from yeast to higher eukaryotes. Peter Hauptmann (Regensburg, Germany) presented a new, Yca1p-independent protease involved in cell death induced by defective N-glycosylation and acetic acid. Although cell death induced by N-glycosylation defects was accompanied by caspase-like activity, this activity seemed to be independent of YCA1. Instead, deletion of the protease KEX1 decreased the caspase-like activity, inhibited ROS formation, and improved cell survival (Hauptmann, 2006). The influence of acetic acid on induced cell death was also reported by Paula Ludovico from Braga, Portugal (Ludovico, 2002). Tobias Eisenberg (Graz, Austria) showed that polyamines promote yeast longevity and could provide the first insights into the mechanism behind it. Daniela Ehehalt (Stuttgart, Germany) delineated perturbations in calcium and manganese homeostasis as inducers of ER stress and programmed cell death in yeast. Heat stress caused impaired degradation of ER-luminal malfolded glycoproteins and subsequent death in cells deleted in PMR1, an ion pump for Ca2+ and Mn2+ uptake, which could be suppressed by the addition of calcium but not of manganese. This ER-linked death program required yeast metacaspase YCA1 and was most pronounced in Δpmr1Δaif1 cells, documenting also the protective role of the yeast apoptosis-inducing factor AIF1. Autophagy is a major intracellular-degradation process that plays a crucial role in survival during starvation in organisms ranging from yeast to mammals. Although autophagy is generally considered to be a nonselective process, selective forms of it have been shown to be involved in the degradation of several organelles. Using lactate-grown yeast subjected to nitrogen starvation, Ingrid Kiššová (Bordeaux, France) was able to provide evidence for selective as well as nonselective mitochondrial autophagy in yeast. The early process of selective targetting of mitochondria was dependent on Uth1p, a mitochondrial outer membrane protein, whereas a late process of classical nonselective microautophagy (including that of mitochondria) was not altered upon deletion of UTH1 (Kissova, 2004). Maïka Deffieu (Bordeaux, France) presented data suggesting that oxidation events play a crucial role in the regulation of mitophagy. Nitrogen starvation to induce autophagy during stationary phase revealed that deletion of the UTH1 gene results in higher levels of mitochondrial protein oxidation, an increase in ROS accumulation and an alteration in fatty acid composition of phospholipids (Kissova, 2006). In recent years, yeast has been successfully established as a model with which to study the functions and mechanisms of various human pro and antiapoptotic proteins involved in cancer development, several neurodegenerative diseases, and AIDS. During this meeting, Peter Polčic (Bratislava, Slovak Republic) presented new insights into the mechanisms that underlie the interactions of Bcl-2 family members. Using yeast as a heterologous expression system to learn about ‘BH3-only’ proteins, he introduced representative ‘BH3-only’ members into yeast and was able to show that these proteins induce cell death in yeast when Bax is coexpressed, indicating that their function can be reconstituted in the yeast system. Stephén Manon (Bordeaux, France) delineated the molecular mechanisms underlying the interaction between Bax and mitochondria during apoptosis. The mobility of the two ends of the protein was demonstrated to be crucial for the conformational change needed in order for it to be targetted to and inserted in the outer mitochondrial membrane. The movement of the C- and N-terminal ends of Bax was shown to enable the protein to uncover the domain (the α1 helix) necessary for interaction with mitochondrial protein(s), thus facilitating its insertion in the mitochondrial outer membrane. In parallel, he was able to demonstrate that the insertion of the hydrophobic C-terminal helix á9 is not required for Bax-insertion. Additional data presented suggest that posttranslational modifications such as phosphorylation of certain residues have an important function in the regulation of the translocation and activation of Bax. In a screen of mammalian cDNA libraries for suppressors of the growth-inhibitory effect of Bax in yeast, Chamel M. Khoury (Montreal, Canada) had identified a novel human antiapoptotic gene product that suppresses Bax-induced yeast cell death independently of the ESCRT (endosomal sorting complex required for transport) pathway. He presented data showing that an alternatively spliced variant of the human VPS24 protein lacking the N-terminal lipid binding domain is not involved in the ESCRT pathway but does serve an antiapoptotic role upon Bax-expression. Using fission yeast as a model system with which to study apoptosis induced by HIV-1 viral protein R (Vpr), Richard Y. Zhao (Baltimore, USA) aimed to gain further insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying Vpr-induced apoptosis. He presented data showing that expression of vpr in fission yeast leads to rapid cell death accompanied by apoptotic chromatin condensation and phosphatidylserine externalization. In yeast, as in mammalian cells, Vpr interrupts the mitochondrial membrane potential in yeast. He further demonstrated that Vpr affects mitochondrial morphology by producing mitochondrial aggregates near the centre of the yeast cell, a phenomenon that could further link to apoptosis. Using the fission yeast model system, two novel antiapoptotic Vpr suppressors, hsp16 or ef2, were identified (Benko, 2004; Zelivianski, 2006). Expression of hsp16 or ef2 not only completely inhibited Vpr-induced cell death and changes of mitochondrial morphology in fission yeast but also suppressed Vpr-induced apoptosis in mammalian cells. Joris Winderickx (Leuven, Belgium) presented novel insights into á-Synuclein-induced toxicity and its effect on longevity and apoptosis in yeast. He showed that expression of synuclein dramatically reduces the chronological life span of yeast cells. Notably, this life-span reduction correlated with the formation of aggregates (Zabrocki, 2005). Frank Madeo (Graz, Austria) presented evidence that yeast Endonuclease G regulates caspase-independent apoptosis and elucidated the pathway necessary for yeast Endonuclease G-mediated cell death. Manuela Côrte-Real (Braga, Portugal) described the first evidence of the requirement of ATP/ADP carrier for mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization and cytochrome c release in yeast committed to apoptosis. She also showed that DNA degradation, comparable to higher-order apoptotic DNA fragmentation in mammalian cells, is linked to yeast apoptosis (Ribeiro, 2006). She also examined the apoptotic modulation of Bcl-2 family proteins by individual mammalian protein kinase C (PKC) isoforms and the regulation of p53-dependent apoptosis by PKC. Karen Sapienza (Msida, Malta) presented data demonstrating the mitochondrial involvement in aspirin-induced apoptosis in yeast cells, a phenomenon of considerable pathophysiological impact (Sapienza & Balzan, 2005). The release of cytochrome c from mitochondria was shown to be an important part of the apoptotic mechanism of aspirin and to occur prior to the disruption of the mitochondrial membrane potential. Using proteomic and cell biological approaches, Paula Ludovico (Braga, Portugal) was able to demonstrate that the TOR pathway is necessary for acetic acid-induced apoptosis. Deletion of two key transcriptional regulators of amino acid synthesis was found to rescue acetic acid-induced yeast cell death. Sergio Giannattasio (Bari, Italy) further delineated yeast programmed cell death triggered by acetic acid. He could demonstrate that, upon acetic acid treatment, yeast follows either a faster YCA1-dependent or a slower YCA1-independent death pathway (Guaragnella, 2006). In addition, he investigated the time course of cytochrome c release into the cytoplasm, providing first insights into the mechanism of this pivotal process in yeast programmed cell death triggered by acetic acid. Birthe Fahrenkrog (Basel, Switzerland) showed that the proapoptotic activity of the nuclear HtrA/Omi-like serine protease Nma111p (Fahrenkrog, 2004) depends on its nuclear localization. She has now identified two nuclear localization signals (NLSs) and one nuclear export signal (NES), and has studied their influence on the ability of Nma111p to mediate yeast apoptosis. Whereas expression of intact Nma111p enhanced apoptotic cell death, a construct mutated in the NLSs showed no hallmarks of apoptosis after induction of cell death using H2O2. Deletion of the NES did not affect cell killing mediated by Nma111p. Campbell Gourlay (Sheffield, UK) presented a defined link between environmental sensing, actin remodelling and apoptosis in budding yeast. He demonstrated that stabilization of the actin cytoskeleton, caused by deletion of SLA1 or END1, induces hyperactivation of the Ras signalling pathway. The consequent rise in cAMP levels leads to the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, accumulation of ROS and death, primarily through a subunit of protein kinase A (PKA). An artificial elevation of cAMP-levels was shown to directly mimic the apoptotic phenotype displayed in actin-stabilized cells. Moreover, he has established a mechanistic link between Ras signalling and actin, by demonstrating that ROS production in actin-stabilized cells is dependent on the G-actin binding region of the cyclase-associated protein Srv2p/CAP. Besides their role in cellular energy metabolism, mitochondria are established and recognized as key players in cell death. Their central role during apoptosis is marked by the release of proapoptotic factors such as cytochrome c and apoptosis-inducing factor (AIF). In yeast, where among others the orthologue of AIF (Wissing, 2004) and apoptotic scenarios such as cytochrome c release (Ludovico, 2002) can be found, mitochondria have advanced to be the main apoptotic organelles. Michael Breitenbach (Salzburg, Austria) introduced the latest advances in the involvement of mitochondria in yeast cell death by delineating the role of two mitochondrial proteins, YGR076cp and Mmi1p. YGR076p, a mitochondrial ribosomal protein, was shown to influence replicative lifespan and to be involved in the TOR pathway, while Mmi1p, the yeast member of the highly conserved eukaryotic gene family TCTP (translationally controlled tumor protein), was demonstrated to shuttle to mitochondria and to colocalize with Rpg1p in so-called stress granules when cells are treated with a mild oxidative stress to induce apoptosis (Rinnerthaler, 2006). Michal Jazwinski (New Orleans, USA) clarified the role of mitochondria in nuclear genome instability and illustrated its relationship with the retrograde response, an intracellular signalling pathway that compensates for age-related mitochondrial dysfunction by inducing the transcription of metabolic and stress-response genes. He also discussed the possibility of an association between age asymmetry and the retrograde response. The meeting was a unique one, not only from a scientific point of view but also on a personal level due to the nice and friendly temper of all participants. The organization by Alena Pichova was perfect, even turning into magic when she brought us into a deep forest near Kutná Hora where the exotic white deer with blue eyes live; they are few but growing in number. After the conference dinner in the empire chateau Kačina, Gennaro D'Urso, a former postdoctorate from Paul Nurse's laboratory, played guitar and sang melting love songs. In one of the conference rest periods we visited an old silver mine, and, seeing how people in Medieval times used to dig 600 m down into the Earth, we realized that the job of a scientist is not that bad, even when working on yeast death is involved. We all look forward to the next meeting, which will be organized by Joris Winderickx during Spring 2008 in the beautiful town of Leuven in Belgium.

title: The role of the MORF/MRG family of genes in cell growth, differentiation, DNA repair, and thereby aging.
abstract: The discovery that replicative cellular senescence is a dominant phenotype over immortality led to the discovery that there are at least four unique genetic subgroups of immortal cell lines that use distinct mechanistic pathways to evade cell cycle exit. Study of one of these genetic complementation groups demonstrated that one gene, MORF4, possessed the ability to induce senescence in group B cell lines. The MRG family of genes, of which MORF4 is a member, has since proven important for cellular aging, proliferation, positive and negative transcriptional regulation, and DNA damage repair. MRG15, the evolutionary ancestor of the family, is highly conserved in yeast, C. elegans, drosophila, plants, and mammals and has been implicated in chromatin remodeling in these species. Our proteomics studies have found that MRG15 is unique among mammalian genes in that it associates with both histone deacetylases and histone acetyl transferase complexes, and thus potentially plays a role in both transcriptional silencing and activation. Its knockout in mice is embryonic lethal, resulting in improper organogenesis, as well as cell proliferation and DNA damage repair defects. Future study of these genes will help clarify the role of chromatin remodeling in aging, cellular proliferation, and DNA damage repair.

title: Transcriptional or post‐transcriptional regulation – how does a plant know when to senesce?
abstract: Plant senescence is familiar to most people in the form of autumn leaf senescence, a process that results in the yellow and red coloration of trees. This process is important for the recycling of nutrients, which would be lost if the old leaves were dropped without prior senescence. One of the best studied individual trees is probably an aspen (Populus tremula) tree on the Umeå University campus (e.g. Keskitalo et al., 2005). In this tree, leaf senescence starts on the same day in September every year. So how does the tree know that it is autumn? This question was addressed by Stefan Jansson (Umeå Plant Science Centre, Sweden) in his introductory lecture of the Third European Workshop on Plant Senescence, organized by Karin Krupinska (University of Kiel, Germany) and Klaus Humbeck (University of Halle, Germany). How autumn leaf senescence and senescence of annual plants are regulated was one of the main topics discussed during the workshop. Other important areas of senescence research that were addressed at the workshop included the processes involved in nitrogen remobilization from senescing leaves and programmed cell death in plants. ‘... initiation of senescence may not be regulated at the transcriptional level and ... induction of SAGs is likely to be a consequence rather than the cause of senescence’ The molecular processes that initiate senescence have occupied scientists for some time. As early as 1980, Thomas and Stoddart (Thomas & Stoddart, 1980) described a ‘temporal discontinuity between the transcription of senescence-specific genes and their expression as the senescence syndrome’, raising the question of whether transcriptional regulation can be responsible for the initiation of senescence. While temperature affects the rate at which aspen leaves senesce, the initiation of senescence is under tight photoperiodic control, preparing the tree for a possible drop in temperature once the days get shorter. Microarray studies conducted by Stefan Jansson's group (Umeå Plant Science Centre, Sweden) revealed that, although the senescence-related decline in chlorophyll starts on the same day each year, changes in the expression of senescence-associated genes (SAGs) do not coincide when different years are compared. This suggests that the initiation of senescence may not be regulated at the transcriptional level and that induction of SAGs is likely to be a consequence rather than the cause of senescence. In contrast to autumn leaf senescence in trees, senescence of annual plants, such as Arabidopsis, is related to reproduction. Microarray studies (e.g. Buchanan-Wollaston et al., 2005; van der Graaff et al., 2006) have revealed a large number of Arabidopsis SAGs, but it is still unclear which of them have a regulatory function. Various approaches are being used to pinpoint regulatory genes, for example Vicky Buchanan-Wollaston's group (University of Warwick, UK) are using systems biology to investigate transcriptional networks in order to identify hubs in the regulation of gene expression. Another group which has focused on identifying transcriptional regulators of senescence is that led by Bernd Müller-Röber (University of Potsdam, Germany). They have analysed the expression of over 2000 transcription factors using quantitative reverse transcription–polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). One member of the group, Salma Balazadeh, presented analysis of a mutant in a senescence-induced transcription factor confirming a role for this transcription factor in senescence regulation. Similarly, WRKY53 has been identified as a senescence regulator (Miao et al., 2004) by Ulrike Zentgraf's group (University of Tübingen, Germany). Transcription of genes during senescence could also be under epigenetic control. While the role of epigenetic control of flowering has been analysed in detail, research on the epigenetic regulation of other life history traits that affect plant fitness (Blödner et al., 2007) is still in its infancy. Klaus Humbeck (University of Halle, Germany) presented exciting results on the importance of epigenetic changes in chromatin structure for the regulation of senescence. Humbeck showed that senescence can be delayed or accelerated, respectively, by overexpression or knock out of a histone methyltransferase. These recent experimental findings using Arabidopsis confirm that transcriptional events play a role in senescence regulation, but to what extent they determine the initiation or only the rate of senescence, once it has been initiated, remains to be shown. Analysis of the proteome of senescing leaves by Shimon Gepstein's group (Technion, Haifa, Israel) has revealed that only half of the genes whose transcript levels are increased during senescence also show up-regulation at the protein level, suggesting a role for post-transcriptional regulation. Perhaps the most intriguing presentation of the workshop discussed a key role for a rare post-translational modification in the regulation of senescence: John Thompson (University of Waterloo, Canada) explained how hypusination of eukaryotic translation initiation factor SA (eIF5A), a protein that recruits mRNAs from the nucleus for protein synthesis, can determine senescence and growth in plants (Duguay et al., 2007). While the hypusinated form probably promotes senescence, the unmodified lysine form of eIF5A promotes plant growth. Manipulation of this post-translational switch provides new opportunities for crop production, for example in extending the shelf life of fruits and enhancing growth. A possible role of protein targeting was described by Karin Krupinska (University of Kiel, Germany). The single-stranded DNA-binding protein Whirly1 from barley, which binds to the promoter of a barley SAG, localizes to the plastids in young flag leaves, but to the nucleus in old flag leaves. The Arabidopsis Whirly protein (AtWhy1) also localizes to the plastid (Krause et al., 2005), but it modulates telomere length in the nucleus (Yoo et al., 2007). In mammalian cells, telomere length is related to senescence, whereas in senescing leaves telomere length is not affected. Nonetheless, modifications in telomere structure may play a role in leaf senescence (Zentgraf et al., 2000). Whereas mutants in AtWhy1 do not show a developmental phenotype, knocking out the Arabidopsis gene for a mitochondrial Whirly protein, AtWhy2, results in delayed senescence, suggesting that protein targeting may be important for senescence regulation. As discussed at the workshop, senescence can be triggered by biotic and abiotic stress. In addition to these environmental factors, internal, age-dependent factors influence senescence by determining the response of plants to their environment. In the Mediterranean perennial plant Cistus clusii, plant age determines the response to drought and high light stress. Sergi Munné-Bosch (University of Barcelona, Spain) presented data showing that, when leaves of the same age originating from plants of different age are compared, the leaves from old plants are found to suffer increased oxidative stress (Munné-Bosch & Lalueza, 2007). Age is also an important component in the senescence response of annual plants. In Arabidopsis, as demonstrated by Paul Dijkwel's group (University of Groningen, the Netherlands), ethylene only induces senescence in plants that have reached a defined age. This treatment has been used to isolate onset of leaf death (old) mutants. The old5 mutant (Jing et al., 2005), which responds early to ethylene treatment and also senesces early in air, was described by Jos Schippers. This mutant is affected in quinolinate synthase, an enzyme that is involved in the synthesis of nicotine adenine dinucleotide (NAD). Metabolic profiling of the old5 mutant revealed changes in primary metabolism. In yeast, NAD has been proposed to play a role in extending lifespan in response to calorie restriction, for example during decreased glucose availability (Lin et al., 2000). In this process, an NAD-dependent histone deacetylase, silent information regulator (Sir2), is required for epigenetic gene silencing. Similar to calorie restriction in heterotrophic organisms, changes in primary metabolism, especially sugar signalling, also play a role in the regulation of leaf senescence (Wingler et al., 2006). At the workshop, this subject was addressed by Thomas Roitsch (University of Würzburg, Germany), who showed how the regulation of cell wall invertase by cytokinin can control senescence. The old5 mutant could now provide a link between changes in metabolism, the epigenetic regulation of senescence and plant age. During the workshop it became clear that plant senescence is regulated at several levels. However, trying to separate the causes and consequences of senescence raises several ‘chicken and egg’ problems. For example, what comes first – transcriptional or post-transcriptional regulation, age or stress, metabolites or gene expression? Latest research makes it possible to suggest a model in which age-dependent changes to chromatin and possibly also telomere structure could make a leaf or a plant competent to react to senescence-inducing environmental stimuli, such as day length or stress (Fig. 1). These stimuli could regulate gene expression either directly or, for example, via plant hormones, metabolites or reactive oxygen species. Changes in metabolism are likely to be the cause as well as the consequence of transcriptional and post-transcriptional changes. Furthermore, a possibly age-related switch in post-translational modification, such as hypusination of eIF5A, could regulate protein synthesis. While downstream processes, such as the degradation of chlorophyll, are highly conserved (Armstead et al., 2007), there are many different ways in which senescence can be induced. Unravelling the causal relationships in the regulatory network therefore remains a challenging task. Hypothetical model for regulatory mechanisms that control senescence in plants.

title: On the Inside
abstract: Alternative RNA processing enables genes to produce a variety of mRNA and protein products, thus expanding the potential informational content of eukaryotic genomes. Recent evidence indicates a high incidence (up to 60%) of alternative splicing (AS) in the human genome, predominantly in the form of exon skip, whereas a minor form is of the type called intron retention (5%–16%). Plants are thought to exhibit less AS, and analyses of AS in Arabidopsis (Arabidopsis thaliana) and rice (Oryza sativa) indicate that intron retention is the most common type of AS in these species. Comparison of AS between different species can provide information about the evolution of AS, the conservation of mechanisms that control AS, and its biological consequences for a species. At the gene level, conservation of AS can provide insights into gene function and the evolutionary history of particular genes and their families. Ner-Gaon et al. (pp. 1632–1641) have developed an algorithm (based on EST pairs gapped alignment) that takes advantage of the relatively small intron and exon size in plants and directly compares pairs of ESTs to search for AS. EST pairs gapped alignment was first evaluated in Arabidopsis, rice, and tomato (Solanum lycopersicum), for which annotated genome sequences are available, and was shown to accurately predict splicing events. The method was then applied to 11 plant species that include 17 cultivars for which enough ESTs are available. The results show a large, 3.7-fold difference in AS frequencies between plant species, with Arabidopsis and rice in the lower range and lettuce (Lactuca sativa) and sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) in the upper range. Hence, compared to higher animals, plants show a much greater degree of variety in the frequency of alternatively spliced genes. In eudicots but not monocots, a correlation between genome size and AS frequency was detected, implying that in eudicots the mechanisms that lead to larger genomes are a driving force for the evolution of AS. Flavonoids, of which more than 6,000 have been identified, are plant secondary metabolites that are widespread throughout the plant kingdom. In nature, flavonoids act as UV light scavengers to protect against oxidative damage, as antimicrobial compounds to defend against pathogens, and as pigments in fruits, flowers, and seeds, where they have a function in attracting pollinators and seed dispersers to facilitate reproduction. Flavonoids are also present in pollen and pistils of many plant species, and there is increasing evidence that flavonoids may play a crucial role in fertility and sexual reproduction. For example, pollination experiments revealed that flavonoids in either the anther or pistil are essential for pollen tube growth, fertilization, and subsequent seed set. To obtain more insight into the role of flavonoids in reproduction and fruit development, Schijlen et al. (pp. 1520–1530) have blocked flavonoid biosynthesis in tomato by RNA interference (RNAi) suppression of the gene encoding chalcone synthase. The resulting transgenic fruits showed a strong decrease of total flavonoid levels and displayed an altered color. More importantly, the fruits were devoid of seeds. The observed parthenocarpic fruit development appeared to be pollination dependent. Fertilization, however, did not occur because chalcone synthase RNAi fruits displayed impaired pollen tube growth. Such seedless fruit phenotypes may prove to be of potential interest to consumers, processing industries, and breeding companies. Because the sites of transcription and translation are physically separated by the nuclear membrane, transcripts must be exported from the nucleus to the cytoplasm through the nuclear pore. The nuclear pore complex (NPC) is constructed from subcomplexes composed of approximately 30 proteins. A major ultrastructural feature of the NPC is the nuclear basket, a filamentous network of proteins that extends from the NPC into the nuclear matrix. The nuclear basket is thought to act as a scaffold for the assembly of various molecules involved in nuclear export. A component of the nuclear basket in vertebrates is TRANSLOCATED PROMOTER REGION (TPR), a large coiled-coil protein associated with inner basket filaments. In a screen for Arabidopsis mutants that suppress the expression of the floral inhibitor FLOWERING LOCUS C, Jacob et al. (pp. 1383–1390) have identified lesions in the Arabidopsis homolog of TPR (AtTPR). In addition to their early-flowering phenotype, attpr mutants display a number of other developmental abnormalities, including reduced size and fertility, occurrence of terminal flowers, and a disorganized cell morphology. A striking molecular phenotype of attpr mutants is the accumulation of polyadenylated (polyA) transcripts in the nucleus. A similar nuclear accumulation of polyA RNA has been reported for mutants in two other Arabidopsis NPC proteins, called SUPPRESSOR OF AUXIN RESISTANCE1 and 3 (SAR1 and SAR3). The nuclear accumulation of polyA RNA suggests that AtTPR is required for the efficient export of RNA from the nucleus. The authors also show that the effects of AtTPR on small RNA abundance and auxin signaling are similar to that of two other NPC-associated proteins, HASTY (HST) and SAR3. These data indicate that attpr, sar3, and hst have similar effects on development, and that early flowering, alterations in auxin sensitivity, and RNA levels may be general phenotypes associated with impaired nuclear pore function. Salicylic acid (SA) has been implicated as a key player in the responses of plants to a wide array of biotic and abiotic stress responses, including systemic acquired resistance. SA has also been demonstrated to reduce plant reproductive fitness, improve seed vigor under stress conditions, induce earlier flowering, and enhance senescence. Despite the apparent involvement of SA in these myriad plant responses, our knowledge of the signal transduction pathways activated by SA is fragmentary. Krinke et al. (pp. 1347–1359) now present evidence that phospholipid signaling may be involved in SA signal transduction. By means of radiolabeled phospholipids, the authors demonstrated that the addition of SA induced a rapid and early (in a few minutes) decrease in a pool of phosphatidylinositol (PI). This decrease paralleled an increase in PI 4-phosphate and PI 4,5-bisphosphate. These changes were inhibited by wortmannin, an inhibitor of type III PI 4-kinases, suggesting that PI 4-kinase is rapidly and transiently activated in response to SA in Arabidopsis suspension cells. The authors also examined the effects of wortmannin on the SA-induced transcriptome. A total of 774 genes were differentially expressed upon SA treatment. The response to SA of 112 of them was inhibited by concentrations of wortmannin sufficient to inhibit PI 4-kinase activity. Seedlings grown at high sugar concentrations show impaired development. This developmental arrest can be overcome by applying the ethylene precursor 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic acid. In keeping with these results, ethylene-insensitive seedlings are found to be more strongly inhibited by Glc in their development than wild-type plants. Moreover, previous studies of Arabidopsis have shown that high abscisic acid (ABA) levels enhance the sensitivity of seedling growth to Glc, and a light-responsive element of a Rubisco promoter responds negatively to both ABA and sugars. Based on the observed cross talk between ethylene, ABA, and sugar signaling in seedling development, Tholen et al. (pp. 1305–1315) have hypothesized that ethylene reduces the negative feedback of carbohydrates on photosynthetic gene expression. Previously, the authors observed a lower rate of whole-plant photosynthesis in ethylene-insensitive Arabidopsis plants containing a dominant-negative mutant allele of the ethylene receptor gene ETHYLENE RESPONSE1. In this study, they switched to a similar ethylene-insensitive version of tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum) because gas exchange can be measured more accurately due to its greater leaf size. They conclude that the inability to perceive ethylene results in an increased sensitivity to Glc, which may be mediated by a higher ABA concentration. This increased sensitivity to endogenous Glc has negative consequences for the Rubisco content and the photosynthetic capacity of these plants. Histone acetylation involves the transfer of acetyl groups from acetyl-CoA to the Lys residues of histones. The hyperacetylation of histones leads to a relaxation of chromatin structure and is associated with transcriptional activation, whereas hypoacetylation of histones induces chromatin compaction and gene repression. The SILENT INFORMATION REGULATOR2 (SIR2) family proteins, also known also as sirtuins, are NAD+-dependent histone deacetylases. Sir2 is involved in chromatin silencing in yeast and is associated with lifespan extension in yeast, worms, and flies. In this issue, Huang et al. (pp. 1508–1519) provide insights into the role of OsSRT1, one of the two SIR2-related genes found in rice. They demonstrate that OsSRT1 is a widely expressed nuclear protein with higher levels in rapidly dividing tissues. Phenotypic and molecular analyses of RNAi transgenic plants suggest that OsSRT1 is involved in the deacetylation of the histone H3 Lys-9 (H3K9) and that it is required for the transcriptional repression of transposable elements and apoptosis-related genes. TUNEL assays and molecular marker gene analysis demonstrated that cell death was induced in OsSRT1 RNAi plants. The TUNEL-positive signals detected in the nuclei of the RNAi leaf cells were indicative of DNA fragmentation similar to that which occurs during programmed cell death and the plant hypersensitive response. The overexpression of OsSRT1 enhanced tolerance to oxidative stress. To study whether the down-regulation of OsSRT1 affected gene expression, the authors compared the transcripts of the RNAi to the wild-type plants by microarray analysis. Such analyses revealed that the transcription of many transposons and retrotransposons as well as genes related to hypersensitive response and/or programmed cell death was activated in OsSRT1 RNAi plants. These findings suggest that OsSRT1 may function in safeguarding plants against genome instability and DNA damage.

title: 2007 Changsha International Symposium on Lupus
abstract: The 2007 Changsha International Symposium on Lupus, co-sponsored by the Institute of Dermatovenereology and the Epigenetic Research Center of the Second Xiangya Hospital at the Central South University was successfully held in Changsha on May 27, 2007. The symposium, having attracted over 500 experts from China, USA, France and Japan, was presided by Dr. LU Qian-jin, Director of the Institute of Dermatovenereology at the Central South University, China. Special lectures were given respectively by Dr. Bruce Richardson from the University of Michigan, USA, Dr. ZHENG Jie from the Shanghai Jiaotong University Medical School, China, Dr. Pierre Youinou from the Brest University Medical School, France, Dr. Eiji Matsuura from the Okayama University, Japan, Dr. Amr Sawalha from the University of Oklahoma, USA, and Dr. HU Nan from the Central South University, China. A great variety of topics were covered including new research developments in the epigenetics of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), the role of B cells in autoimmunity as well as oxidative stress in the pathogenesis of SLE, and the latest advances in the clinical management of cutaneous lupus erythematosus. The symposiums pointed out the international research trends on lupus and exhibited the latest developments in both basic and clinical researches. SLE is an autoimmunol disorder harming the physical health of people. The etiology of SLE is still unknown. The spotlight of the symposium was the research achievements on the epigenetic pathogenesis of SLE. Epigenetics has gradually become a heated research field in recent years with relevant research fruits growing exponentially. Epigenetics is defined as the study of heritable changes in gene function that occur without a change in the sequence of nuclear DNA. Epigenetic mechanisms include DNA methylation, histone modifications (acetylation/deacetylation, etc), microRNAs that modify gene expression, and perhaps the developing area of nuclear domains. DNA hypermethylation and histone hypoacetylation are hallmarks of gene silencing, while DNA hypomethylation and acetylated histones promote active transcription. Dr. Bruce Richardson outlined the important role for DNAmethylation abnormalities in the development of SLE. Abnormal hypomethylation of total genomic T cell DNA was found in active lupus and lupus-like diseases. T cells treated with DNA methylation inhibitors became autoreactive in vitro and resulted in autoimmunity in vivo by increasing LFA-1 (CD11a/CD18). Other methylation sensitive T cell genes include perforin, CD70, IgE FcRγ1, CD40L, and KIRs. It was observed that the promoter regions of these genes were demethylated in T cells from patients with active SLE. Demethylation of these sequences can contribute to increased promoter activity, and thus could lead to the gene's overexpression. Functional studies showed that demethylation of the CD11a promoter could cause T cells to be autoreactive, demethylation of perforin promoter may participate in the spontaneous monocyte/macrophage killing that characterizes lupus T cells, demethylation of the CD70 promoter results in increased B cell costimulatory and immunoglobulin overproduction, and demethylation of IgE FcRγ1 promoter could lead to abberant SLE T cell signal transduction. Dietary folate or methionine restriction may worsen DNA demethylation in lupus. Decreased ERK pathway signaling, due to oxidative damage, may result in Dnmt1 expression decreasing, contributing to DNA demethylation in lupus. The reason why lupus occurs more frequently in women than in men is unknown. “While estrogen contributes to the predisposition, other observations, such as young girls getting lupus more frequently than young boys, indicate that other factors contribute,” said Dr. LU Qian-jin. Recent research by Lu and his collaborators pointed to the “awakening” of a woman's inactive X chromosome as a potential culprit. Women have two X chromosomes; one is inactivated by processes including DNA methylation. CD40-ligand (CD154, CD40LG), a B cell costimulatory molecule, is aberrantly overexpressed on T cells in lupus, potentially contributing to autoantibody overproduction. CD40lg is encoded on the X chromosome. Regulatory sequences on the inactive X chromosome demethylate in T cells from women with lupus, contributing to CD40LG overexpression uniquely in women. Demethylation of CD40LG and perhaps other genes on the inactive X may contribute to the striking female predilection of this disease. Dr. Amr Sawalha discussed how decreased ERK signaling in T cells results in DNA hypomethylation and autoimmunity. Dr. Sawalha generated a transgenic mouse expressing a dominant negative MEK1 in T cells using a tetracycline-inducible expression system. The ERK signaling defect reduced Dnmt1 expression in T cells, and overexpression of the methylation sensitive genes CD11a and CD70. However, the methylation sensitive gene CD40L was only overexpressed in female mice. CD70 was overexpressed in MRL/lpr mice as compared to age and sex matched MRL+/+ controls. Bisulfite DNA sequencing revealed hypomethylated CG pairs in the CD70 gene in MRL/lpr mice at 16 weeks compared to 5 weeks. The findings suggest that abnormal DNA methylation due to decreased expression of Dnmt1 in CD4+ T cells is associated with the loss of immune tolerance and age dependent autoimmunity in MRL/lpr mice. This validates the MRL/lpr lupus-prone mouse as a model system to test potential therapeutic interventions that can alter DNA methylation or block the CD70/CD27 pathway in lupus. Indeed, the preliminary results indicate that blocking CD70 using a monoclonal anti-CD70 antibody improves skin and kidney disease in MRL/lpr lupus-prone mice. If confirmed, the findings suggest that interfering with CD70/CD27 interaction could be a novel therapeutic approach to human lupus. Dr. HU Nan discussed abnormal histone modification patterns in lupus CD4+ T cells. Global histone H3 and H4 hypoacetylation was found in CD4+ T cells from patients with active lupus compared to controls. There was a negative correlation between global histone H3 hypoacetylation and disease activity. In addition, global histone H3K9 hypomethylation was found in both active and inactive lupus CD4+ T cells compared to controls. However, global levels of H3K4 methylation was not different between patients and controls. Human SIRT1 controls various physiological responses including cell fate, stress, and aging, through deacetylation of its specific substrate protein. SIRT1 mRNA levels were significantly increased in active lupus CD4+ T cells compared to healthy controls. The findings suggest that both histone acetylation and histone methylation are abnormal in CD4+ T cells from SLE patients. Dr. Pierre Youinou discussed the revival of B cells in autoimmunity. The subpopulations of B cells may be classified according to three criteria: ontogenesis, the sequence passing through the germinal center (GC), and the expression of CD5. B cells are also classified according to their membrane expression of CD5. The BCR response is ultimately tuned by a handful of coreceptors: CD19 for example diminishes the threshold of the response, and CD5 increases this threshold and leads to anergy of autoreactive B cells. B cells have, in fact, been endowed with another three tasks. They act as efficient Ag presenting cells (APC), produce cytokines in the form of B effector (Be)1 releasing for example interleukin (IL)-2 or Be2 releasing IL-4. One of these B-cell-induced cytokines is the B cell-activating factor of the tumor necrosis family, referred to as BAFF. This survival factor for B cells is central to the pathogenesis of autoimmune diseases, but also to that of CLL. B cells are involved in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), SLE and primary Sjögren's syndrome (SS), not only as Ig-making PC, but also as APC. Dr. Pierre Youinou's group has established that the alternate exon 1 of CD5 is normally repressed. One of the mechanisms for silencing such a gene is its methylation by DNA methyltransferases (DNMT). Activation-induced methylation of B cells might not function properly in autoimmune settings, based on a deficiency of DNMT. Dr. Eiji Matsuura discussed the clinical significance of antiphospholipid antibodies and autoimmune-accelerated atherosclerosis. The interaction between oxLDL and β2GPI in the intima to form their complexes strongly suggests that this complex is an atheroantigen. This interaction has been well characterized and the oxLDL-derived ligands specific for β2GPI was identified. APS patients may produce the antibodies of these complexes, resulting their circulating immune complexes trigger atherosclerotic changes. The physiologic relevance of this finding has been demonstrated in vitro by the enhanced macrophage uptake of IgG immune complexes of oxLDL/β2GPI. The participation of macrophage Fcγ receptors in the uptake of the IgG immune complexes seems to be particularly important in the development of foam cells and atherosclerotic plaques in APS. Many studies shed some light on H. pylori infection causing not only chronic disease in the stomach, such as gastritis ulcer, and MALT lymphoma, but also atherosclerosis. H. pylori activates resident macrophages and lymphocytes in the gastric mucosa, followed by induction of systemic immune responses against Hp-HSP60. Circulating Hp-HSP60 specific T lymphocytes are turned into Th1-dominant T lymphocytes by interacting with antigenic endogenous HSP60 molecules expressed on the endothelium of arteries. The differentiated Th1-dominant T lymphocytes penetrate in the intima. They contribute to the macrophage derived-foam cell formation by activating macrophages to develop atherosclerosis in patients with such a chronic disease. Dr. ZHENG Jie discussed common and rare skin eruption features of acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (ACLE), subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE) and chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CCLE), as well as the latest advances in the clinical management of CLE. CLE is divided into LE-specific skin disease and LE-nonspecific skin disease. Vesiculobullous skin change in LE is one of the LE-nonspecific lesions. The risk of patients presenting with classic DLE lesions to subsequently develop into SLE is between 5% and 10%. Roughly one-fourth of patients with SLE develop DLE lesions at some point in the course of their disease, which prognosticates that such patients tend to have less severe forms of SLE. The diagnosis of CLE is on the basis of clinical manifestation and histopathology; moreover ACLE, SCLE, and some DLE also need examination for autoantibodies. Systemic corticosteroids are not as a rule prescribed during the treatment of CLE. The scientific program of this symposium covered cutting-edge development in basic research and the latest advance of clinical management of lupus.

title: Phenomics, Lamin A/C, and Metabolic Disease
abstract: Characterizing the molecular genetics and defining the clinical phenotypes of the lamin A/C-related disorders, collectively referred to as “laminopathies,” has been one of the most intriguing chapters in human genetics (1). Lamins are intermediate filament proteins that reside normally on the inside of the nuclear envelope and perform numerous biological functions including maintenance of structural integrity, organization of chromatin, governing division of nuclear contents during mitosis and meiosis, and regulation of access of transcription factors to the nucleus (2). In the last 10 yr, mutations in the genes encoding these proteins have been shown to underlie a breathtaking array of human illnesses, including inherited muscular dystrophies, peripheral neuropathies, cardiomyopathies with conduction disturbances, and disorders of accelerated aging (1). However, for endocrinologists, the subgroup of laminopathies that has held the greatest fascination has been those with a primary metabolic phenotype, specifically Dunnigan-type familial partial lipodystrophy subtype 2 (FPLD2; MIM 151660), which results from heterozygous mutations in LMNA encoding lamin A/C (3). The partial lipodystrophy syndromes are associated with insulin resistance, multiple quantitative metabolic disturbances, and ultimately diabetes. FPLD2, which although very rare is still probably the most prevalent of the inherited lipodystrophies, is characterized by sc lipoatrophy of arms, legs, gluteal region, and abdomen, with lipohypertrophy of visceral fat stores, upper truncal fat, and neck and facial fat (4). The identification of LMNA as the causative gene for FPLD2 required classical linkage analysis studies which showed that genetic markers on chromosome 1q21 perfectly segregated with the FPLD2 phenotype (5). This statistically implicated this region of the genome as harboring the causative gene for FPLD2 (5). Subsequent detailed analysis of genes residing within 1q21 was performed using automated sequencing of genomic DNA of members of a Canadian FPLD2 family. These studies revealed a novel heterozygous missense mutation in exon 8 of LMNA, namely p.R482Q (6). The list of causative mutations in FPLD2 was rapidly expanded soon thereafter, but the overwhelming majority of FPLD2 mutations were found in LMNA exon 8, especially codon 482, with missense mutations p.R482Q, p.R482W, and p.R482L (7). Presently, most newly diagnosed North American patients with FPLD2 have one of these codon 482 mutations. Virtually all FPLD2 subjects with codon 482 mutations had a pure “classical” FPLD2 phenotype, with minimal involvement of other tissues, such as skeletal or cardiac muscle. We have since noted that the FPLD2 phenotype seemed milder in carriers from pedigree branches that were remote from the proband and her immediate nuclear family. Partial lipodystrophies have been closely scrutinized using a wide range of technologies. A key approach has been “phenomic” analysis of molecularly characterized individuals. Phenomics has been defined as systematic application of clinical, biochemical, and imaging methodologies—tools that are familiar to practicing clinicians and clinician investigators (8). But while a practicing clinician might have incentives to minimize the amount of technology expended to make the correct diagnosis, a human genetics investigator, even with constrained research funding, sometimes has the luxury to apply diagnostic technologies more extensively, albeit strategically, to identify subtle clinical phenotypic differences. These “deep phenotypes” are often quantitative, so that differences between individuals with well-characterized genotypes can be evaluated statistically. Characterizing phenotype-genotype correlations in patients can be more technically challenging, resource-intensive, and artifact-prone than studying them in animal models. But there are also advantages when studying phenotypic consequences of mutations in patients, including the fact that the landscape of background genetic and environmental factors—compared with, say, transgenic mouse models—can be more appropriate when attempting to translate experimental findings of potential relevance to human disease. For instance, careful phenomic evaluation of FPLD2 kindreds showed the initial metabolic insult to be insulin resistance followed closely by dyslipidemia, then hypertension, then diabetes, and finally vascular disease (3). The clarified progression of abnormal phenotypes in FPLD suggested a rational, staged treatment regimen to possibly modulate the natural history and development of disease end points (3). Furthermore, understanding the stages of disease progression might not only have value for rare FPLD2 patients, but could also help in understanding the metabolic evolution of common insulin resistance or metabolic syndrome (MetS). More recent investigations of LMNA and lipodystrophy have followed three experimental paths. First, powerful molecular genetic technologies have continued to define new laminopathies resulting from new LMNA mutations. Some recently characterized multisystem laminopathies, such as Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome, atypical progeroid syndromes, and mandibuloacral dysplasia, also had partial lipodystrophy as a component phenotype (1). In retrospect, it is not surprising that certain LMNA mutations lead to complex syndromes that include partial lipodystrophy as one of the elements. Second, genomic DNA sequencing experiments expanded to allow evaluation of other candidate genes, particularly in patients with a suggestive phenotype but no germline LMNA mutations. Such experiments uncovered heterozygous dominant negative and haploinsufficiency mutations in PPARG (3, 4) encoding peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ. The resulting phenotype was called FPLD3 (MIM 604367) and was characterized by prominent insulin resistance but less dramatic lipoatrophy of extremities, concurrent with preservation of abdominal sc fat and relatively less visceral adiposity compared with FPLD2 (3). The AKT2 gene has also been implicated in some cases (9). Finally, with reduced barriers to automated DNA sequencing, the net for mutation detection is being cast much more widely. Genomic interrogation of LMNA has been extended to include large numbers of subjects without classical FPLD2, but instead with more subtle—even clinically undetectable—partial lipodystrophy together with nonclassical adipose tissue involvement or with overlapping syndromes involving multiple organs and tissues. For instance, in the current issue of JCEM, Decaudain et al. (10) have extended the range and characterization of LMNA-associated metabolic phenotypes by screening the genomic DNA of 277 unrelated adults with a range of phenotypes, including lipodystrophy and/or android body habitus, insulin resistance, or altered glucose tolerance. They found LMNA mutations in only approximately 10% of patients, indicating molecular heterogeneity of the complex “relaxed” phenotype. They found typical FPLD2 LMNA codon 482 mutations in 17 patients (6.2%). However, in 10 patients (3.6%) they found a total of nine additional heterozygous LMNA non-codon 482 mutations: eight of these were missense mutations (two in exon 1, five in exon 7, and one in exon 9), and one was a frameshift mutation (in exon 11). Ex vivo experiments provided evidence of dysfunction for at least some of the mutations. They then grouped patients into those with and without codon 482 mutations. Their comprehensive phenomic analysis has led to some new insights. First, they noted that the LMNA codon 482 and non-codon 482 mutation patient groups each had a high proportion of subjects with insulin resistance and hyperglycemia, diabetes, hypertension, menstrual irregularities, and elevated plasma triglycerides. Second, they found several key differences between the groups: non-codon 482 mutation carriers had milder lipoatrophy—three did not even have clinically apparent lipoatrophy—with higher BMI and larger waist circumference, and relative sparing of limb, trunk, and total fat stores. The milder lipoatrophy was confirmed by medical imaging studies, which showed that non-codon 482 mutation carriers had less atrophy of sc fat on the thighs and sparing of abdominal sc fat together with smaller visceral fat stores compared with codon 482 mutation carriers. The milder adipose redistribution in non-codon 482 mutation carriers was associated with older age at diagnosis, delayed onset of metabolic disturbances, and less severely depressed plasma leptin and HDL cholesterol. Also, sc lipomas and more severe acanthosis nigricans appeared to be more prevalent among codon 482 mutation carriers than among non-codon 482 mutation carriers. The authors named the clinical syndrome in non-codon 482 mutation carriers “metabolic laminopathy” (MLP), a phenotype that is clearly distinct from typical FPLD2. In fact, MLP appears to more closely resemble FPLD3 (3), especially with respect to the pattern of adipose redistribution, which is less severe than in FPLD2 but is still associated with insulin resistance and a wide range of quantitative metabolic disturbances. Of interest was whether subjects with these laminopathies met criteria for MetS. Some FPLD2 patients studied by Decaudain et al. (10) appeared not to have MetS, at least not by waist circumference criteria proposed by the International Diabetes Federation (IDF). In contrast, because of sparing of abdominal sc fat, all MLP (like most FPLD3) patients met the IDF waist circumference criteria for MetS. Parenthetically, FPLD2 patients provide an example of how increased waist circumference is not always crucial—perhaps thus not mandatory—to diagnose MetS, because FPLD2 patients met other defining criteria for MetS, including dyslipidemia, dysglycemia, and blood pressure, not to mention insulin resistance and diabetes. FPLD2 illustrates how criteria that depend on a mandatory waist circumference threshold might sometimes misclassify individuals as “unaffected” despite expanded visceral fat stores, which a simple tape measurement would not ascertain because of concomitant atrophy of abdominal sc fat. Patients with partial lipodystrophy represent the ultimate in vivo“experiment-of-nature” with regard to human adipose tissue development and dysfunction. The differences in adipose tissue distribution between FPLD2 due to LMNA codon 482 mutations and MLP due to non-codon 482 mutations might lead to the identification of molecular pathways and programs that underlie varying degrees of lipodystrophy correlated with varying degrees of clinical involvement. An unresolved question is whether the metabolic disturbances in partial lipodystrophy develop secondarily to adipose tissue repartitioning or result from a direct effect of the mutant gene product. The phenomic studies of Decaudain et al. (10) suggest that the less extreme fat redistribution in MLP is associated with less extreme biochemical perturbations, although the temporal relationship between the onset of fat repartitioning and metabolic changes is not clear. However, the examples of FPLD2 and MLP indicate how combining genomic and phenomic perspectives can guide future experiments and perhaps improve understanding of common clinical entities, such as MetS or HIV-associated partial lipodystrophy. They also indicate that experiments in which the entire murine Lmna locus is ablated, even in a tissue-specific manner, might fail to capture the pathogenetic subtlety that is suggested by the clearly divergent phenotypes that result from single nucleotide mutations in human LMNA. Thus, the concept of phenomics reinforces the value of clinical acumen and evaluative skills in phenotypic assessment. The current environment in molecular genetic research places a sizeable premium on the recapitulation of human phenotypes in animal models. Although these models have often proved helpful in moving our understanding of molecular pathways and targets forward, a large proportion of transgenic or knockout models fails to produce relevant and informative phenotypes for investigation of human disease. It is likely that careful phenomic evaluation of phenotypes in humans—as well as mice—will become an even more important component of biomedical research in the postgenomic world. title: A Combination of Genomic Approaches Reveals the Role of FOXO1a in Regulating an Oxidative Stress Response Pathway
abstract: BACKGROUND: While many of the phenotypic differences between human and chimpanzee may result from changes in gene regulation, only a handful of functionally important regulatory differences are currently known. As a first step towards identifying transcriptional pathways that have been remodeled in the human lineage, we focused on a transcription factor, FOXO1a, which we had previously found to be up-regulated in the human liver compared to that of three other primate species. We concentrated on this gene because of its known role in the regulation of metabolism and in longevity. METHODOLOGY: Using a combination of expression profiling following siRNA knockdown and chromatin immunoprecipitation in a human liver cell line, we identified eight novel direct transcriptional targets of FOXO1a. This set includes the gene for thioredoxin-interacting protein (TXNIP), the expression of which is directly repressed by FOXO1a. The thioredoxin-interacting protein is known to inhibit the reducing activity of thioredoxin (TRX), thereby hindering the cellular response to oxidative stress and affecting life span. CONCLUSIONS: Our results provide an explanation for the repeated observations that differences in the regulation of FOXO transcription factors affect longevity. Moreover, we found that TXNIP is down-regulated in human compared to chimpanzee, consistent with the up-regulation of its direct repressor FOXO1a in humans, and with differences in longevity between the two species.
