title: Proteomic Identification of Plasma Proteins Associated with Future Dementia Development
abstract: Dementia is a progressive decline of cognitive abilities, severe enough to affect daily life activities and independent function. Dementia is most common in older individuals: about one-third of adults 85 years or older may exhibit Alzheimer disease (AD) related dementia, but it is not a normal part of aging (1). Various neurodegenerative disorders contribute to the development of dementia through progressive and irreversible loss of neurons and brain function. AD accounts for 60%–80% of dementia cases (1). Amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles are key pathological features of AD. Amyloid beta 42 and p-tau are known biomarkers for the presence of AD pathology and therapeutic targets (2). However, these AD biomarkers do not appear to be well suited on their own for determining the risk of developing AD dementia before amyloid pathology or related cognitive symptoms appear. Furthermore, therapies targeting these pathologies have shown modest but not complete clinical improvement of cognitive symptoms. While our knowledge regarding biomarkers for AD and other dementias has increased dramatically in recent years, a better understanding of biological pathways that may lead to development of dementia, and the identification of potential associated biomarkers, may enable the selective application of preventive measures including therapeutic interventions and lifestyle changes. Current known risks for dementia include, but are not limited to, nonmodifiable factors such as age and genetics. For example, the risk of AD dementia and vascular dementia increases with age; while the most significant genetic risk factor for sporadic AD is the presence of the apolipoprotein E gene APOE4 (3). The reason APOE4 increases AD risk is not well understood and inheriting APOE4 does not ensure on its own that the individual will develop AD. Modifiable risk factors of dementia include smoking, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease (4). AD is characterized by a long asymptomatic preclinical phase in which the individuals appear to be cognitively normal (CN) but have evidence of amyloid pathology (2). However, many CN individuals presenting with amyloid pathological changes never develop AD dementia using current cognitive assessments. This further highlights the need to identify new biomarkers and therapeutic targets for long-term dementia risk stratification and disease progression. One way to achieve this is by employing proteomic methods to retrospectively identify proteins that are differentially expressed in individuals who developed dementia versus those who do not. While proteomic studies have been undertaken to identify potentially clinically relevant proteins, most previous studies have focused on identifying risk factors in individuals in a time frame relatively close to disease onset. Walker et al. undertook a multifaceted approach to identify relative plasma protein abundance associated with the development of dementia in individuals 45 to 65 years of age, often decades prior to the development of dementia related symptoms (5). In a primary proteomic discovery analysis, 1784 individuals who developed dementia over the course of a 25-year follow-up period were retrospectively identified out of 10 981 participants in the Atherosclerosis Risk in Community study cohort. This provided a large cohort for SomaLogic’s SomaScan v.4 proteomic analysis utilizing 5284 nucleic acid-based protein binding aptamers to query the association of the abundance of 4877 plasma proteins with long-term neurocognitive outcomes. However, some potential drawbacks of aptamer-based biomarker discovery include overrepresentation of secreted proteins, cross-reactivity with nonintended target proteins, and target protein affinity variations related to protein complexing or single nucleotide polymorphisms. Using this initial proteomic analysis, a total of 32 proteins were associated with future development of dementia (Table 1). After adjusting for known risk factors (APOE4 status, cardiovascular disease, and kidney dysfunction), 26 proteins were found to be associated with the development of dementia within 25 years. Seven proteins were found to be associated with the development of dementia within 15 years as determined by an internal replication study on the original study cohort. Only one protein, Growth/Differentiation Factor-15 (GDF-15), was found to be associated with dementia risk in both the 25-year and 15-year groups. Further work was then performed to better elucidate the potential clinical relevance of the 32 proteins identified by the initial proteomic analysis. Two independent secondary study external replication cohorts were used to attempt to reproduce the association of the discovered proteins with dementia development and to evaluate their association with known CSF biomarkers of AD pathology, neurodegeneration, and neuroinflammation. Fifteen of the 32 originally identified proteins were associated with the development of dementia in at least one of the 2 replication cohorts via SomaScan abundance assessment of 4877 proteins. To assess for potential differential protein expression in brain tissue of AD patients, some (but not all) protein expression patterns in post mortem brain tissues versus control brain tissues were examined in 2 patient cohorts. Eight unique proteins, denoted as + in Table 1, were identified to be differentially expressed in AD patient brain tissue as compared to control brain tissue in at least one cohort. Additional studies were conducted to evaluate the expression of the identified proteins in brain tissue, to assess the biological pathways and protein networks linked with the identified proteins, and Mendelian randomization analysis and genome-wide association studies to assess association with AD, and plasma protein abundance. While these various studies did not uniformly indicate association of all proteins with dementia, several proteins were associated with CSF markers of AD (amyloid beta and p-tau) and/or associated with non-AD specific markers of neurodegeneration (including total-tau and neurofilament light chain). Four of the identified proteins are prioritized AD therapeutic targets; 8 proteins are targets of non-AD existing drugs; and 3 of the proteins have been genetically linked to AD (Table 1). The protein that exhibited the strongest association with 25-year dementia risk was GDF-15, but this immune and stress response protein does not appear to be linked to an AD specific role and was not associated with CSF amyloid and/or p-tau concentrations. This extensive analysis identified 4 potentially overlapping functional pathways, previously known to be associated with long-term development of dementia: proteostasis, immunity, synaptic function, and extracellular matrix organization (ECMO). Fifteen of the 32 originally identified proteins were classified as “prioritized midlife biomarkers of dementia risk and AD” and placed into one of the 4 functional pathways by the authors (see Table 1). While the degree of risk associated with these proteins and associated pathways for the development of dementia is not currently fully understood, these results may spur further investigation into mechanisms that lead to dementia development. For example, the authors suggest a causal relationship for dementia development for the immune-related proteins serpin family A member 3 (SERPINA3) and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), as well as an association of alteration of the extracellular matrix organization related metalloproteinase proteins such as MMP12 and MMP19, with long-term AD risk. Two synaptic proteins appeared to function as midlife markers of AD-related dementia (cerebellin 4 precursor (CBLN4) and glutamate ionotropic receptor delta type subunit 2 (GRID2)). The proteostasis-related proteins such as the heat shock protein heat shock protein family A (Hsp 70) member 1B (HSPA1B), and the chaperone proteins DNAJ Heat Shock Protein Family DNJB9/DNAJB12, were associated with long-term AD dementia risk and the authors suggest that up-regulation of these proteostasis proteins may occur in response to the presence of protein misfolding before the development of dementia. Using a subset of 13 of these proteins, the authors developed a predictive model for the development of future all-cause dementia. This model only achieved a ROC curve (AUC) of 0.66. This predictive model significantly underperformed when compared to a predictive model that included a combination of known risk factors (such as age, APOE4 status, cardiovascular risk factors) with an AUC of 0.77 in the patient cohort. Combining both predictive models did not improve the performance of either model alone. This data indicates that while the identified proteins may be altered in individuals developing dementia later in life; at present they do not represent strong long-term prognostic biomarkers. Furthermore, the remaining challenges in the predictive power of the long-term markers is evident in comparison to the clinical performance of emerging CSF and circulating biomarkers for the evaluation of the presence of amyloid-related pathology, which often exhibit AUCs >0.90 (2). The impressive amount of evidence generated by Walker et al. will require future effort to fully understand and confirm the relevance of their findings to dementia risk and AD pathogenesis, as many of these proteins have some function unrelated to neurological-specific processes. It should be noted that dementia in the original proteomic cohort was not specific to AD and may have been related to other types of dementia or mixed dementias. Furthermore, SomaScan aptamer technology does not detect all potential proteins within the proteome, and indeed, a newer version of SomaScan (not utilized in this study) has expanded the number of protein abundance targets to 7288. However, it is comforting that proteomic analysis did identify multiple proteins previously identified of pathological/therapeutic interest in AD. While this study yielded novel information regarding biological pathways that may lead to dementia development, it remains to be determined as to how these proteins and pathways might lead to the development of dementia much later in life. Further examination of these proteins and pathways may eventually (but not immediately) translate into advances in targeted early intervention. title: The times are changing: A primer on novel clinical trial designs and endpoints in critical care research
abstract: Critical care medicine has been a rapidly evolving area of clinical practice since its inception.1 This rapid evolution, supported by scientific and technological advancements, has been further propelled by evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs).2 The RCT has been the gold-standard approach for establishing cause and effect.2 This study design provides the most effective control of confounding by baseline variables, thus addressing the most important threat to establishing cause-and-effect relationships between an intervention and outcome of interest. Overall familiarity of the research community, ease of interpretation, and ability to provide a high-quality answer to a specific research question have facilitated increasing use of RCTs in critical care research. As the number of critical care RCTs has increased over time, several challenges have been identified.2,3 First, substantial heterogeneity of disease and severity of illness presents a unique challenge for trial enrollment, outcome evaluation, and bedside applicability. Second, rapidly obtaining informed consent and deploying an intervention is very different, and often more difficult, within critical care medicine as compared to other practice areas. Third, poor prognosis in many critically ill conditions, such as sepsis, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and cardiac arrest, presents greater potential for futility.4-6 Furthermore, selecting an optimal trial outcome can be difficult as clinical practicality and applicability must be considered alongside what is important to the patient. Lastly, the standard approach to trial design often creates a rigid and inflexible infrastructure, furthering research inefficiency. Collectively, these factors have contributed to numerous RCTs across a spectrum of critically ill populations and interventions producing neutral results, leading to calls for novel RCT methodology.2,7-13 Furthermore, single-center RCTs producing positive results are frequently overturned by subsequent larger, multicenter RCTs.14 This primer for the clinical pharmacist will discuss innovative clinical trial designs and novel trial endpoints within critical care research. Within each section, emerging approaches aimed at overcoming the challenges and limitations of traditional methodologies will be discussed. Furthermore, practical examples and available resources will be highlighted to assist clinical pharmacists in understanding, interpreting, and applying these methodologies in their clinical practice and/or research. Although growing rapidly, critical care medicine as a specialty remains on the younger end of the spectrum when compared to other fields of medicine and, as such, remains behind in terms of designing and conducting resource-efficient clinical trials. Notable challenges in critical care research and how each contributes to decreased trial efficiency and applicability are summarized in Table 1. In the following section, we provide an overview of alternative study designs that can be utilized to overcome the limitations of traditional RCTs along with examples of their application. Notable Limitations of Study Designs of Traditional RCTs2 Abbreviation: RCT, randomized controlled trial. Issues with applicability and feasibility in RCTs arise when trial protocols are overly restrictive and do not reflect true clinical practice.2,15 This complicates not only trial enrollment and proceedings but also application of trial protocols or results to the “gray areas” of practice at the bedside. Therefore, pragmatic trial designs are of interest within critical are research.16 Trial pragmatism (ie, the degree to which trial enrollment and intervention delivery reflect real-world practice) exists as a continuum rather than a dichotomy, and the PRagmatic-Explanatory Continuum Indicator Summary-2 (PRECIS-2) is a validated tool developed to help evaluate this continuum.17 The PRECIS-2 utilizes 9 domains to assist trialists in evaluating the impact their design decisions will have on applicability. Pragmatic trial designs can be used to better align clinical research and clinical practice, improving efficiency and applicability. Trial embedment is one approach to enhancing pragmatism. In these designs, recruitment, enrollment, randomization, interventions, data extraction, and/or documentation are integrated into existing clinical practice.18,19 For example, a study on stress ulcer prophylaxis utilized a registry-embedded component to improve ascertainments.20 In a trial examining the effect of procalcitonin monitoring on antibiotic use, guidelines were embedded as a decision support tool within the electronic heath record, which increased protocol compliance and presented a change easily translatable to clinical practice.21 Another approach to pragmatism is the cluster RCT, which can be a parallel or stepped-wedge design depending on whether crossover of clusters is utilized (Figure 1).22 Cluster RCTs have been used to study fluid balance control in critically ill patients.23 Additional examples utilizing parallel, stepped-wedge, and other pragmatic designs have been produced by Vanderbilt University Medical Center and the Pragmatic Critical Care Research Group.24 Together, they have enrolled more than 40,000 patients across 15 trials focusing on airway management, fluid management, and antibiotic selection.25-28 Cluster RCTs provide a more efficient design when interventions are best applied to patient groups (eg, patients within an intensive care unit [ICU], healthcare institution, or health system) rather than at the individual patient level. They can reduce crossover between intervention and control groups, enhance external validity, and facilitate evaluation of interventions targeting modification of healthcare environments or behaviors.29,30 Depiction of parallel and stepped-wedge cluster randomized controlled trial (RCT) study designs. Parallel cluster RCTs (top panel) are randomized at the center (eg, ICU, clinic, hospital) level rather than the individual level. Centers (clusters) are randomized to control (shaded blue) or treatment (shaded gray) for the duration of the study (in parallel). Data are collected continuously throughout the study on all clusters. Data from the treatment and control groups are compared in statistical analysis. Stepped-wedge cluster RCTs (bottom panel) are randomized at the center (eg, ICU, clinic, hospital) level rather than the individual level. The study begins with all centers (clusters) exposed to control (shaded blue). Clusters are the randomized to cross over to treatment exposure (shaded gray) at regular intervals (steps). This occurs until all participants have crossed over and experienced the treatment. Data are collected continuously throughout the study on all clusters during both control and treatment time periods. Data from the treatment and control groups are compared in statistical analysis. In contrast to parallel cluster RCTs, wherein clusters are randomized to treatment or control at baseline and only a subset of enrolled clusters receive treatment, stepped-wedge cluster RCTs involve all clusters receiving treatment, with the chronological sequence of treatment allocation across clusters being randomly allocated. Stepped-wedge designs may be better suited to examine complex interventions in a more timely and accurate manner due to the gradual (ie, stepwise) participant recruitment into the intervention.22 This can be especially helpful in critical care medicine when research to inform clinical practice is needed but logistical or operational barriers exist. A drawback of stepped-wedge versus parallel cluster RCTs is greater vulnerability to confounding from changes in practice over time.31 With either cluster RCT design, clustering must be clearly justifiable before conducting a trial with this design.29,30 Additionally, the statistical analysis must account for correlation of outcome risk among patients within the same clusters compared to those from other clusters. Oversimplification of trial interventions (ie, investigating only one or two of many possible alternative interventions) is especially common in critical care research.2 Consider acute ischemic stroke, which can be managed with fibrinolytics, antiplatelets, statins, and/or procedural interventions at varying doses, time points, or durations. Multiple RCTs looking at these interventions individually could be (and have been) conducted. However, a multifactorial design, or the study of multiple interventions within the same trial, can be a more efficient way to investigate several of these interventions at once (Figure 2).19 Examples of multifactorial designs include the FACTT trial in ARDS (conservative vs liberal fluids and pulmonary artery catheter vs central venous catheter) and the VANISH trial in septic shock (vasopressin vs norepinephrine and hydrocortisone vs placebo).32,33 Both studies compared multiple combinations of multiple types of interventions, decreasing the need to repeat individual RCTs. Additionally, there was an increased likelihood trial participations would receive at least some type of active therapy, as opposed to only placebo, due to combinations of interventions. One challenge with multifactorial designs is potentially complex trial protocols, depending on the number of interventions under investigation. Additionally, a common concern with multifactorial designs is potential interactions between multiple interventions, which could make interpretation and application of results challenging.19 Depiction of a multifactorial randomized controlled trial (RCT) study design. Patients enrolled are randomized to a treatment regimen. Each treatment regimen is a combination of different interventions of interest (Treatments 1-3 and Treatments A and B). The multifactorial design allows for each combination of interventions to be studied. Following randomization, patients are exposed to their assigned treatment regimen and data are collected. Data from each of the treatment regimen groups are compared in statistical analysis. The need to answer multiple questions has always existed in critical care research; however, the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic further emphasized the timeliness with which researchers needed to do so and led to the growing use of adaptive trials (Figure 3).34,35 Adaptative in this context refers to changing of a component of trial design after the trial has started (eg, refining sample sizes, abandoning ineffective treatment arms, adjusting patient populations for inclusion, or changing randomization ratios).2,35 A common feature of adaptive trials is response-adaptive randomization, which involves adjusting randomization ratios based on accumulating trial data. This cyclic process continues until a predefined success or futility threshold is met and the study concludes. Bayesian statistical methods are used in adaptive designs because of their ability to handle continuous assessment of accumulating evidence in addition to what is known prior to trial commencement.2,36 The utility of Bayesian analysis has also been demonstrated in post hoc analyses of RCTs originally reporting neutral findings whereby the application of a Bayesian approach suggested a signal of benefit.37 Further discussion on Byesian analysis has been published elsewhere and is beyond the scope of this primer.37,38 Depiction of an adaptive randomized controlled trial (RCT) study design. Patients enrolled are randomized to treatment and control groups, as they typically would be in a traditional RCT. Data are collected on each group over a period of time. During a preplanned interim analysis, accumulated trial data is analyzed and used to modify aspects of the ongoing trial, which in this example is randomization ratio. Preplanned thresholds for trial success and/or futility can also be assessed at an interim analysis to determine if the trial should proceed. Trial modifications are made if needed, and patients enrolled will continue with their assigned treatment. This can occur over repeated interim analyses until trial completion. Data are collected continuously throughout the trial and compared in statistical analysis. Platform trials are an extension of adaptive trials and are another way to investigate multiple treatments in a specific condition.39 Platforms are broad categories or domains of interventions aimed at treating a specific condition, with each platform composed of specific therapeutic agents or combinations thereof. Platform trials can be classified as open or closed.39 Closed platforms consist of a set number of interventions and have a definite stopping point. Alternatively, open platforms begin with a set number of interventions but have the ability to add or drop interventions or platforms based on adaptive rules. This creates a perpetual study design that can be continued as new hypotheses are developed or interventions are identified.40 To date, few critical care trials have used adaptive platform designs; however, with methodological and technological improvements, they are gaining traction in both adult and pediatric populations.41,42 One well-known example is the REMAP-CAP study.43 Although initially designed to study treatments for the adaptive platform was to to interventions for The ongoing REMAP-CAP study platforms for and with the ability to add platforms as new are the platform trial was during the pandemic and facilitated and of multiple clinical trials to potential effective trials have led to the of other adaptive platform trials the of within critical care research that are or will be within the platform trials have often in of specific study due to futility thresholds being of futility can treatment and Furthermore, of randomization ratios can potentially the sample needed to statistical improving trial include the ability to patient the ability to modify treatments or treatment groups over time, and the potential for in trial However, challenges also complex trial protocols and infrastructure, statistical and substantial and resources which use of adaptive platform trials. improving the design and efficiency in critical care research will in of such evidence must be into clinical practice to impact patient The in of is and the need for than focusing on the effect of a clinical these trials investigate interventions to improve of in clinical care and examine the between and the of the are few published critical however, there is an ongoing trial investigating of care and within the With growing for the of and its application to trials will a in critical care research to the bedside. title: Improving healthspan among people with sickle cell disease: Leveraging precision health in an era of treatments with curative intent
abstract: With the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval of two new cell-based gene therapies (Casgevy, Lyfgenia) for sickle cell disease (SCD) on December 8, 2023,1 gene therapies and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) are heralded as the next era of potentially curative treatments for people born with sickle cell disease (SCD).2, 3 Despite these groundbreaking advances, which have been accelerated by the discovery of clustered regularly interspaced palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-Cas9 gene-editing technology,2, 3 there are still persistent shortcomings that preclude improved quality of life among many people born with SCD.4, 5 Notable examples of remaining challenges include the need for endpoints of functional cure as recently reviewed by Locatelli et al,6 informative surrogate biomarkers of specific severe complications that translate to tailored clinical decisions for each patient, as well as the availability, accessibility, and equity of clinical management and treatments.4, 5, 7 The current utilization of SCD treatments with curative intent is limited, even in higher-income settings.2, 8 HSCT2 is costly, requiring specialized facilities and clinical expertise as well as lengthy in-patient hospitalization. Allogeneic HSCT ideally involves human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-matched hematopoietic stem cells to minimize graft versus host disease risk. HSCT is often only provided to people with severe disease, since transplantation has substantial risks including graft failure, infection, infertility, and death.9, 10 Aside from Casgevy and Lyfgenia, other gene therapies have been evaluated as preclinical models3 and additional clinical trials are ongoing. Most gene therapy protocols require myeloablative conditioning, which increases the risk of secondary malignancies. Second, among people who successfully receive HSCT or gene therapies for the treatment of SCD, there are a host of emergent questions regarding new risks, long-term monitoring, and clinical management (Figure 1). Short-term physiologic questions are to determine the extent that SCD-associated damage to multiple organs is reversible, which will inform clinical management of the risk for specific clinical sequelae from irreversible damage. In the longer-term, there is a need for improved and ongoing risk monitoring across the life span of every individual. Given genetic variability across human populations,20 off-target effects from gene-editing remain an active area of investigation.10 Safety concerns from off-target effects, the unintended alteration of gene expression of other untargeted genes, include genotoxicity and genomic instability due to altered chromosomal rearrangements.10 Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI)-based predictive modeling21 and data integration tools for multi-omics,22 minimally-invasive biomonitoring via wearable technologies,23, 24 and microfluidic assays for rheological properties of red blood cells and blood accumulation25 could be adapted and jointly leveraged for future personalized clinical management of SCD. Machine-learning and data-driven network approaches can simultaneously account for joint distributions and conditional dependence between multiple disparate data types (e.g., clinical signs and symptoms, laboratory assessments, treatments, comorbidities, omics data, psychosocial and behavioral factors).21, 22 This is advantageous for more accurately reflecting the heterogeneous disease progression, especially acute and chronic complications, among people with SCD. Predictive models, in combination with multi-omics data, have tremendous potential26 for a deep characterization of each SCD patient. The identification of robust biomarker signatures could shed light on the key underlying pathophysiologic pathways of individual treatment responses, leading to improved precision, efficiency, and cost-effectiveness of treatments. Large-scale multivariate data approaches could provide systematic, efficient screening of candidate biomarkers, which are critical—albeit initial—steps. Subsequent steps will include the extensive validation of reproducibility and accuracy in diverse populations, and evaluation of the translation to actionable clinical insights and utility. Other major challenges to fully leverage the potential of AI and multi-omics include the: standardization of collection (e.g., biological samples, SCD symptom and treatment history, timepoints); harmonization of omics assays including genetics; coordination of larger, statistically powered longitudinal studies with longer follow up duration among people with SCD prior to and after receiving potentially curative treatments. Historically, individuals with SCD have faced stigma and discrimination resulting from the improper handling of their personal data.27 Consequently, it is essential for all researchers to prioritize and incorporate current best practices in artificial intelligence ethics, including data privacy, ethical use of data, equitable accessibility of treatments and AI benefits, as well as evaluating and minimizing potential bias of AI models.28 As we enter this next era of SCD treatment, precision health approaches have considerable potential to provide earlier and accurate risk assessment of clinical sequelae, and thereby, an improved capacity for a longer healthspan among people with SCD. The continued expansion of SCD treatment options is providing a long-awaited opportunity to improve our ability to identify the right SCD treatment for the right patient at the right time. title: Genome-wide CRISPR screens identify PTPN21 and WDR26 as modulators of the mitochondrial stress-induced ISR
abstract: Dear Editor, Organisms have evolved mitochondrial stress response pathways to surveil mitochondrial function and activate repair programs upon detection of mitochondrial dysfunction [1]. Failure to respond to mitochondrial perturbation has been implicated in aging and age-related diseases [2, 3]. Mitochondrial perturbation in mammals primarily activates the integrated stress response (ISR), in which four kinases—HRI (haem-regulated inhibitor or eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2 alpha (eIF2α) kinase 1 (EIF2AK1)), PERK (PKR-like ER kinase), GCN2 (general control nonderepressible 2), and PKR (protein kinase RNA-dependent)—mediate the phosphorylation of eIF2α [4–6]. eIF2α phosphorylation selectively elevates the translation of a subset of transcripts, including those encoding the transcription factors ATF4 (activating transcription factor 4) and CHOP (C/EBP homologous protein) [7, 8]. Since the gene that encodes CHOP is also a target of ATF4 [9], transcription of CHOP is also upregulated. Here, we employed genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screens to identify potential regulators of the ISR during mitochondrial stress in mammalian cells. We then focused on tyrosine-protein phosphatase nonreceptor type 21 (PTPN21) and WD repeat-containing protein 26 (WDR26), two of the candidate genes from the screen. Knockdown of PTPN21 or WDR26 suppressed the induction of ISR upon mitochondrial perturbation. Mechanistically, PTPN21 and WDR26 facilitated the interaction between DELE1 (death-associated protein 3 (DAP3)-binding cell death enhancer 1) and HRI, thereby relaying the mitochondrial stress signal to the cytosol. Deficiency of PTPN21 or WDR26 impaired cell fitness upon challenge with mitochondrial stressors. These findings pave the way to understanding the mechanisms underlying the mitochondrial stress-induced ISR in mammalian cells. To identify potential factors that mediate the mitochondrial stress-induced ISR in mammalian cells, we sought to perform an unbiased genetic screen with the use of CRISPR/Cas9 technology. As previously reported, treating 293T cells with different mitochondrial inhibitors—paraquat, antimycin, or carbonyl cyanide m-chlorophenyl hydrazone (CCCP)—induced the expression of the transcription factor CHOP [10, 11] (Fig. 1a–c; Supplementary Fig. S1a). We then performed immunostaining using a commercial antibody against CHOP and found that the fluorescence signal was greatly induced when cells were treated with the mitochondrial stressor antimycin (Supplementary Fig. S1b). Fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) successfully separated untreated or antimycin-treated cells based on CHOP fluorescence intensity (Supplementary Fig. S1c). Most importantly, when CHOP knockout cells were treated with antimycin, they showed same FACS profile as untreated cells (Fig. 1d). We then performed FACS-based genome-wide CRISPR screens in the presence of antimycin to identify positive and negative regulators of the mammalian mitochondrial stress response (Fig. 1e). The top and bottom 5% of the cells were sorted out based on CHOP fluorescence intensity. Genomic DNA was extracted, PCR-amplified, and subjected to sequencing for single guide RNA (sgRNA) enrichment analysis (Fig. 1e). Two datasets were generated based on our analysis, showing the normalized abundance of each sgRNA in two biological replicates within the “Ctrl” and “CHOP-low” or “CHOP-high” groups (Supplementary Tables S1 and S2). Candidate genes were picked based on the following criteria: the normalized sgRNA count in the “Ctrl” dataset was not < 7, and the sgRNA was enriched over 2-fold in both biological replicates. Notably, while we were working on this project, two elegant studies were published using similar CRISPR approaches to monitor the induction of ATF4 or CHOP and search for regulators of ISR [12, 13]. Both studies identified a previously less-characterized protein, DELE1, which transduces mitochondrial stress signals to the cytosol to activate HRI kinase and initiate ISR. Encouragingly, in our screen, DELE1 and HRI were also identified to be required for the induction of CHOP (Fig. 1f; Supplementary Table S1). These results indicate that our CRISPR screens successfully uncover regulators of the mitochondrial stress-induced ISR in mammalian cells. Paraquat inhibits the function of mitochondrial complex I, antimycin is an inhibitor of mitochondrial complex III, and CCCP is an uncoupler of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. (b) Immunoblotting analysis showing that different mitochondrial inhibitors induce the expression of CHOP. Paraquat, 0.5 mg/mL 12 h; antimycin, 50 μg/mL 12 h; CCCP, 10 μmol/L 12 h. (f) Genome-wide screens uncover regulators of the mitochondrial stress response in mammalian cells. The positive fold changes represent genes enriched in the “CHOP-low” group. Among the candidate genes, we first focused on PTPN21 because the fold enrichment of this gene was high and knockdown of PTPN21 by small interfering RNA (siRNA) or short hairpin RNA (shRNA) indeed impaired the induction of CHOP at both the protein and mRNA levels when cells were challenged with antimycin (Fig. 2a and b; Supplementary Fig. S2a and b). In addition, knockdown of PTPN21 resulted in suppression of CHOP induction when cells were treated with other mitochondrial inhibitors such as CCCP and oligomycin (Supplementary Fig. S2c–f). Furthermore, deficiency of PTPN21 inhibited the induction of ATF4, another transcription factor involved in the ISR (Supplementary Fig. S2g). Expression of PTPN21 in PTPN21-knockdown cells restored the induction of CHOP (Fig. 2c), excluding the possibility that the small RNAs generate off-target effects. Importantly, deficiency of PTPN21 not only disrupted the induction of CHOP and ATF4, but also impaired the upregulation of multiple genes that are involved in the mitochondrial stress response (Fig. 2d; Supplementary Fig. S2h) [14, 15]. To further explore the function of PTPN21 in mitochondrial stress-induced ISR, we searched the BioGRID database to see whether any PTPN21-associated proteins were also identified in our CRISPR screen. WDR26, a protein that interacts with PTPN21, was uncovered by our screen. Interestingly, the interaction between WDR26 and PTPN21 was enhanced upon mitochondrial perturbation (Fig. 2e). Knockdown of WDR26 by siRNA or shRNA also inhibited the induction of CHOP and ATF4 under mitochondrial stress conditions (Fig. 2f; Supplementary Fig. S2c–g). Overexpression of WDR26 dramatically enhanced the expression of CHOP in WDR26-deficient cells (Fig. 2g). More importantly, the upregulation of the ISR induced by overexpression of PTPN21 or WDR26 was completely blocked by knockdown of the corresponding other gene (WDR26 or PTPN21), suggesting that these two proteins collaboratively modulate the ISR in response to mitochondrial stress (Fig. 2h). Additionally, knockdown of WDR26 impaired the induction of other mitochondrial stress response genes (Fig. 2i; Supplementary Fig. S2h and i). Conversely, knockdown of PTPN21 or WDR26 did not impair the induction of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress marker gene BIP (binding immunoglobulin protein) (Supplementary Fig. S2j). Moreover, knockdown of PTPN21 or WDR26 did not inhibit the activation of the ISR induced by nutrient deprivation (Supplementary Fig. S2k). Taken together, these results indicate that PTPN21 and WDR26 play important roles in the mitochondrial stress-induced ISR in mammalian cells. In mammalian cells, mitochondrial dysfunction promotes the cleavage of DELE1 protein by mitochondrial protease OMA1 (overlapping with the m-AAA protease 1 homolog), resulting in accumulation of cleaved DELE1 in the cytosol, where it associates with HRI and stimulates the kinase activity of HRI to phosphorylate eIF2α (Fig. 3a) [12, 13]. Enhanced eIF2α phosphorylation then facilitates the translation and expression of CHOP [8]. In line with these discoveries, treating cells with an ISR inhibitor (ISRIB), which reverses the effects of eIF2α phosphorylation, or overexpression of GADD34 (growth arrest and DNA damage-inducible protein 34, a phosphatase of eIF2α), resulted in the suppression of CHOP induction upon antimycin treatment (Fig. 3b; Supplementary Fig. S3a). In addition, the elevated induction of CHOP in PTPN21-overexpressing cells treated with antimycin was compromised by ISRIB or GADD34 overexpression (Fig. 3b; Supplementary Fig. S3a). More importantly, knockdown of PTPN21 or WDR26 suppressed the induction of eIF2α phosphorylation and enhanced global protein synthesis upon mitochondrial inhibition (Fig. 3c and d). These data suggest that PTPN21 and WDR26 function upstream of eIF2α phosphorylation during the mitochondrial stress-induced ISR. PTPN21 and WDR26 promote the interaction between DELE1 and HRI. Consistent with previously published results [12, 13], when cells were treated with the mitochondrial inhibitors antimycin or CCCP, DELE1 started to accumulate in the cytosol (Supplementary Fig. S3b and c), and cytosolic accumulation of DELE1 was blocked by knockdown of the mitochondrial protease OMA1 (Fig. 3e). Knockdown of PTPN21 or WDR26 did not alter the mitochondrial localization of DELE1 under normal conditions (Supplementary Fig. S3d), or the cytosolic accumulation of DELE1 under mitochondrial stress conditions (Fig. 3e). In addition, unlike OMA1, knockdown of PTPN21 or WDR26 did not prevent the cleavage of DELE1 (Fig. 3f and g). Furthermore, expression of DELE1 lacking the mitochondrial targeting sequence (DELE1ΔMTS) dramatically elevated the expression of CHOP, even in the absence of mitochondrial inhibitors (Fig. 3h; Supplementary Fig. S3e). Knockdown of WDR26 or PTPN21 suppressed the induction of CHOP in cells overexpressing DELE1ΔMTS (Fig. 3h; Supplementary Fig. S3e). These results indicate that PTPN21 and WDR26 function after the cleaved DELE1 accumulates in the cytosol. Consistent with these findings, we observed that PTPN21 and WDR26 constantly localized in the cytosol, regardless of the presence or absence of mitochondrial stress inducers (Supplementary Fig. S3f). To further dissect the site of action of PTPN21 and WDR26, we performed epistatic analysis to see whether they functioned upstream or downstream of HRI. Overexpression of PTPN21 or WDR26 elevated CHOP expression in antimycin-treated cells (Fig. 3i and j). However, the upregulated expression of CHOP in cells overexpressing PTPN21 or WDR26 was compromised by knockdown of HRI or DELE1 (Fig. 3i–l). Once cleaved DELE1 accumulated in the cytosol, it interacted with HRI to transduce the mitochondrial stress signal (Supplementary Fig. S3g). Based on the above findings, we then tested whether PTPN21 and WDR26 affected the interaction between DELE1 and HRI. Knockdown of PTPN21 or WDR26 indeed suppressed the interaction between DELE1 and HRI (Fig. 3m and n). Taken together, these results indicate that PTPN21 and WDR26 facilitate the interaction between HRI and cleaved DELE1, thereby activating HRI to phosphorylate eIF2α and promote CHOP expression (Supplementary Fig. S3h). Consistent with the important roles of PTPN21 and WDR26 in mediating the mitochondrial stress-induced ISR, knockdown of PTPN21 or WDR26 greatly altered mitochondrial morphology when cells were challenged with the mitochondrial stressor antimycin. Upon antimycin treatment, PTPN21 or WDR26 knockdown cells exhibited more extensive mitochondrial morphology disruption compared to wild-type cells. This suggests a reduced resilience and capacity in these cells to manage mitochondrial damage (Fig. 4a and b). Knockdown of HRI, PTPN21, or WDR26 also modestly affected mitochondrial respiration, as evidenced by the reductions in basal respiration, maximal respiration, and ATP production (Supplementary Fig. S4a and b). These results suggest that these proteins play a fundamental role in maintaining mitochondrial functionality in the cells. PTPN21 and WDR26 regulate mitochondrial physiology and cell fitness. Mitochondrial stress responses, often induced in tumor environments by conditions like nutrient deprivation or hypoxia, lead to essential cellular adaptations and metabolic reprogramming for cancer cell survival and proliferation [17]. Given this context, we explored whether WDR26, important in mitochondrial stress-induced ISR, impacted the anchorage-independent growth of cancer cells. title: Pygo-F773W Mutation Reveals Novel Functions beyond Wnt Signaling in Drosophila .
abstract: Pygopus (Pygo) has been identified as a specific nuclear co-activator of the canonical Wingless (Wg)/Wnt signaling pathway in Drosophila melanogaster . Pygo proteins consist of two conserved domains: an N-terminal homologous domain (NHD) and a C-terminal plant homologous domain (PHD). The PHD's ability to bind to di- and trimethylated lysine 4 of histone H3 (H3K4me2/3) appears to be independent of Wnt signaling. There is ongoing debate regarding the significance of Pygo's histone-binding capacity. Drosophila Pygo orthologs have a tryptophan (W) > phenylalanine (F) substitution in their histone pocket-divider compared to vertebrates, leading to reduced histone affinity. In this research, we utilized CRISPR/Cas9 technology to introduce the Pygo-F773W point mutation in Drosophila , successfully establishing a viable homozygous Pygo mutant line for the first time. Adult mutant flies displayed noticeable abnormalities in reproduction, locomotion, heart function, and lifespan. RNA-seq and cluster analysis indicated that the mutation primarily affected pathways related to immunity, metabolism, and posttranslational modification in adult flies rather than the Wnt signaling pathway. Additionally, a reduction in H3K9 acetylation levels during the embryonic stage was observed in the mutant strains. These findings support the notion that Pygo plays a wider role in chromatin remodeling, with its involvement in Wnt signaling representing only a specific aspect of its chromatin-related functions.

title: Deciphering the Causal Relationships between Blood Metabolites and Coronary Atherosclerosis: A Comprehensive Mendelian Randomization Study
abstract: Objective: This study aims to investigate the causal relationships between specific blood metabolites and the risk of coronary atherosclerosis using a two-sample Mendelian Randomization (MR) approach. Methods: We utilized genome-wide association summary statistics from 8,299 participants in the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA) and 456,348 participants from the UK Biobank to examine 1091 blood metabolites and 309 metabolite ratios. Instrumental variables (IVs) were identified based on genetic variants strongly associated with these metabolites and ratios, and a robust set of IVs was employed to ensure the validity of the MR analyses. Various MR methods, including Inverse Variance Weighted (IVW), MR-Egger, and Weighted Median approaches, were used to address different assumptions and potential biases.

title: The importance of continuing development of novel animal models of Alzheimer's disease and Alzheimer's disease and related dementias
abstract: The development of the first mouse models of Alzheimer's disease (AD) in the mid-1990s was recognized as a significant advance in the research field. These models use transgenic overexpression of single mutations in human amyloid precursor protein (APP) or presenilin 1 (PS1). The APP mutation models like the PDAPP and the Tg2576 mice developed age-related amyloid beta (Aβ) deposition, ultimately resulting in amyloid plaques. The mice transgenic for human PS1 mutations did not demonstrate amyloid deposition; however, when crossed with an APP mutation transgenic mouse, the PS1 mutation led to more rapid deposition of amyloid and significant cognitive impairment at earlier ages than the APP mutation mice alone. These findings led to the combination of APP and PS1 mutations in single mouse models, such as the 5XFAD transgenic mice, harboring three human APP mutations and two human PS1 mutations. This mouse rapidly develops amyloid deposition, within just a few months after birth. Most recently, instead of using transgenic overexpression of mutated human genes, knock-in technologies have now introduced the human APP sequence in place of the mouse APP gene, and include one or more of the mutations associated with early-onset familial AD. These knock-in mouse models provide more physiologically relevant insights because the gene expression is under the normal regulation of the gene and does not include multiple copies of the gene of interest. Disease insights have been significantly advanced as a result of the mouse models harboring familial AD mutations in APP, PS1, and PS2. This includes leading to the development of the first successful disease-modifying therapies for AD in the form of monoclonal anti-Aβ antibodies. However, the mouse models are not complete models of AD. In fact, despite the enormous burden of amyloid deposition that occurs in these models, there is little-to-no neurodegeneration and no obvious neurofibrillary tangle (NFTs)—the other pathology, in addition to amyloid plaques, needed for diagnosis of AD. Therefore, the models are reflective of cerebral amyloidosis as opposed to frank AD. The development of models for NFTs has primarily focused on transgenic overexpression of mutant human tau; however, these mutations that are found in the mouse models of NFTs are not associated with AD, but rather frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and related tauopathies. Since the discovery of early-onset familial AD genetic mutations, many risk genes for sporadic AD have been identified including TREM2 and apolipoprotein E ε4, among many others. Also, many lifestyle risk factors for later-life AD and AD and related dementias (ADRDs) have been identified including diet, exercise, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes. With the advances in our understanding of sporadic AD and the heterogeneity of AD and ADRDs across individuals, it is clear that there is a need for the development of novel animal models of AD and ADRDs that reflect the heterogeneity, the genetic risks of sporadic disease, and the multi-morbidity in our aging population at risk of AD and ADRDs. Such animal models will also be critical for more efficacious pre-clinical drug testing for late-onset AD/ADRDs in a precision-medicine–based strategy. It was this need that led the National Institute on Aging to fund the creation of the two Model Organism Development and Evaluation for Late-onset Alzheimer's Disease (MODEL-AD) Centers: one at the University of California Irvine (UCI) and one at a collaboration between Indiana University (IU), The Jackson Laboratories (JAX), and the University of Pittsburgh (PITT). Important aspects of the MODEL-AD program include the generation of novel models; the rigorous characterization of the models by pathologic, imaging, and multi-omic approaches; the development of a robust preclinical testing pipeline; as well as full, open, data sharing through SAGE Bionetworks and sharing of the models through the JAX repository. The MODEL-AD consortium is part of a larger translational research pipeline to help speed the development of novel therapeutics for AD/ADRD that also includes the Accelerating Medicines Partnership for Alzheimer's Disease (AMP-AD), the Target Enablement to Accelerate Therapy Development for Alzheimer's Disease (TREAT-AD, which will be the focus of a future special issue), and early stage clinical development programs. This special issue encouraged the submission of articles from the MODEL-AD Center scientists, but also from the broad research community who may be leveraging the novel models. The goal of the special issue is to highlight the exciting advances being made in the development of model organisms for the study of AD and ADRDs, and to inform the field of the breadth of resources MODEL-AD provides to the research community, enabling improved translation of research findings to the clinic.

title: Studies on Human Cultured Fibroblasts and Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinomas Suggest That Overexpression of Histone Variant H2A.J Promotes Radioresistance and Oncogenic Transformation.
abstract: Background: Cellular senescence in response to ionizing radiation (IR) limits the replication of damaged cells by causing permanent cell cycle arrest. However, IR can induce pro-survival signaling pathways that reduce the extent of radiation-induced cytotoxicity and promote the development of radioresistance. The differential incorporation of histone variant H2A.J has profound effects on higher-order chromatin organization and on establishing the epigenetic state of radiation-induced senescence. However, the precise epigenetic mechanism and function of H2A.J overexpression in response to IR exposure still needs to be elucidated. Methods: Primary (no target, NT) and genetically modified fibroblasts overexpressing H2A.J (H2A.J-OE) were exposed to 20 Gy and analyzed 2 weeks post-IR for radiation-induced senescence by immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence microscopy. Transcriptome signatures were analyzed in (non-)irradiated NT and H2A.J-OE fibroblasts by RNA sequencing. Since H2A.J plays an important role in the epidermal homeostasis of human skin, the oncogenic potential of H2A.J was investigated in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC). The tissue microarrays of cSCC were analyzed for H2A.J protein expression pattern by automated image analysis. Results: In response to radiation-induced DNA damage, the overexpression of H2A.J impairs the formation of senescence-associated heterochromatin foci (SAHF), thereby inhibiting the SAHF-mediated silencing of proliferation-promoting genes. The dysregulated activation of cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases disturbs cell cycle arrest in irradiated H2A.J-OE fibroblasts, thereby overcoming radiation-induced senescence. Comparative transcriptome analysis revealed significantly increased WNT16 signaling in H2A.J OE fibroblasts after IR exposure, promoting the fundamental mechanisms of tumor development and progression, including the activation of the epithelial-mesenchymal transition. The quantitative analysis of cSCCs revealed that undifferentiated tumors are associated with high nuclear H2A.J expression, related with greater oncogenic potential. Conclusion: H2A.J overexpression induces radioresistance and promotes oncogenic transformation through the activation of WNT16 signaling pathway functions. H2A.J-associated signatures may improve risk stratification by identifying patients with more aggressive cSCC who may require radiotherapy with increased doses.

The authors established 57 organoids from 73 GC patient specimens, covering multiple stomach sites and different TNM stages. A detailed histopathologic analysis confirmed that PDOs recapitulated the histologies of their original tumors in a subtype-specific manner. For example, PDOs derived from intestinal-type GC were characterized by single-layered or cribriform glandular morphologies, featuring cells arranged to form multiple luminal structures of variable dimensions. In comparison, those derived from diffuse-type GC presented with loosely-cohesive to solid cell clusters or cystic configurations. Despite some inconsistencies, these data underscore that organoid cultures maintain the histopathologic features of their parental GC tumors. The team then investigated the responsiveness of GC PDOs to 6 common chemotherapeutics for GC patients. The authors rigorously assayed drug sensitivity by independent measurements (AUC values and IC50 values) across 2 different passages of each organoid line and along 2 sets of drug concentrations. After ensuring the robustness of the assay, they analyzed RNA sequencing data to correlate gene expression changes with drug responsiveness variability in matched PDOs. Pathway enrichment analysis revealed upregulation of the p53 signaling pathway and cellular senescence in 5-FU-sensitive PDOs. By contrast, 5-FU-resistant PDOs showed strong enrichment of tumor-invasion- and stemness-related pathways, such as NOTCH signaling and WNT signaling. Similarly, signaling pathways enriched for PDOs with differential responses to oxaliplatin were also identified. From significantly enriched pathway genes, several were selected for functional experimentation to test for their contribution to drug responsiveness. Notably, knockout of MSMB or S1PR4 (5-FU-sensitive genes) by CRISPR-Cas9 editing significantly decreased the sensitivity of PDOs to 5-FU treatment. Conversely, knockout of FKBP10 (a 5-FU-resistant gene) conferred sensitivity to 5-FU treatment on PDOs. Likewise, genes involved in oxaliplatin response (MYO1A and NDUFA4L2) were also validated. These results are significant since they demonstrate the biological regulation of these genes on chemotherapeutic sensitivity in GC PDOs. Employing the recursive feature elimination method, the researchers explored gene-expression-based biomarkers that discriminated sensitive PDO lines from lines that were resistant to 5-FU treatment. A panel of 9 genes was identified and verified to have high discriminative AUC values. Similarly, a panel of 6 genes was established to predict responsiveness to oxaliplatin treatment. These predictive gene signatures were further validated using The Cancer Genome Atlas cohort, wherein patients treated with 5-FU or oxaliplatin were stratified into sensitive- and resistant-like groups based on gene signature scores. Notably, in the 5-FU-treated cohort, sensitive-like patients showed significantly better progression-free survival. This 5-FU gene signature also showed the highest AUC values for predicting drug sensitivity when compared against published gene signatures. To validate the drug response data obtained ex vivo, the authors established matched PDO xenograft (PDOX) in immunodeficient mice for chemotherapeutic treatment. Importantly, in each of the 5 PDO-PDOX paired models, drug responsiveness was highly consistent between in vitro and in vivo assays. The PDO drug testing results were further subjected to the last, perhaps most important, validation using real-life clinical outcome data from original GC patients. Specifically, 12 PDO-matched patients received peri- or postoperative adjuvant chemotherapy with oxaliplatin and 5-FU and were followed for up to 49 months. Strikingly, 11 out of 12 patients exhibited drug response results consistent with their corresponding PDO lines. These data highlight that PDOs are robust and valid tools for cancer drug screening and drug response prediction. Lastly, the authors explored the impact of the tumor microenvironment on drug responsiveness by co-culturing cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) with autologous PDOs. Indeed, the presence of CAFs substantially increased the drug resistance of PDOs to 5-FU and oxaliplatin treatment. Interestingly, this pro-resistance effect was also seen when PDOs were co-cultured with heterologous CAF lines. These findings align with the recognized role of CAFs in enhancing drug resistance within the tumor microenvironment.10Saw P.E. Chen J. Song E. Targeting CAFs to overcome anticancer therapeutic resistance.Trends Cancer. 2022; 8: 527-555https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trecan.2022.03.001Abstract Full Text Full Text PDF PubMed Scopus (79) Google Scholar In summary, upon establishing a sizable PDO biobank for GC patients, this study identified and verified genes and molecular signatures that are predictive of chemotherapeutic response. Co-culturing with CAFs highlighted the role of the tumor microenvironment in mediating drug resistance. These results confirm the robustness of PDO models for cancer drug screening and response prediction. Moving forward, single-cell multi-omic analyses of PDOs will identify mechanisms underlying drug responsiveness in an unprecedented resolution. Moreover, single-cell CRISPR screening on PDO models will causally pinpoint genes responsible for drug resistance in an unbiased manner. These exciting new molecular technologies, together with sophisticated organoid modeling of the tumor microenvironment, will greatly improve precision medicine for cancer patients.
